speechtext:
This question involves answers that it has never been regarded in the public interest to give. The right hon. leader of the apposition will remember that on a somewhat similar occasion he took the view that he could not disclose what transpired in council. There is no trouble about the numbers of the orders in council. The difficulty is with regard to the question as to when the orders in council are regarded as having passed. Two questions are asked:	when
approval was given, and when the order in council passed council. On one occasion in a court of law I remember when the clerk of the privy council was called he was told that he need not answer the question, on what date did the council sit? Those are hardly questions pertinent to the conduct of the executive government, and I think the question should be dropped.
Question dropped.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
notice in a Canadian Press despatch of June 19 the following appears as a statement by the Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson). I quote from the Evening Citizen of that date:
The dominion government is willing to increase its contribution to the costs of caring for transient unemployed from one-third to one-half of the total, Senator Gideon Robertson, federal Minister of Labour, announced last night.
I should like to ask the government if that is a correct statement of policy with respect to the matter referred to?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Senator Robertson has
not yet returned to Ottawa, but I am in a position to say that a temporary arrangement of that sort has been made with the western cities. It is purely a temporary arrangement.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext:
I notice that
the Minister of Labour is also reported as having remarked that:
-some $2,000,000 of the relief funds remained unexpended and may be used to meet the present situation.
May I point out that when this house was considering the bill for the appropriation of $20,000,093 at the special session last September, the Prime Minister himself moved the following amendment, which was adopted by the house:
Any portion of the said sum of twenty million dollars remaining unexpended or unappropriated for the purposes of this act on the 31st day of March, 1931, shall thereupon lapse.
I assume that the Minister of Labour may not have had that particular section of the act in mind when he made his announcement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext: The Minister of Labour had that in mind. His announcement refers to that portion of the $20,000,000 that was appropriated but unexpended; that is, it was appropriated for direct relief, and a portion of that money still remains unexpended. The whole particulars were laid upon the table within the first fifteen days of the session.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext: I do not wish to argue the point at the moment, but certainly a reference to Hansard shows very clearly that my right hon. friend led the house to believe it was intended that commitments prior to the end of the fiscal year in the nature of payments that would have to be made of known amounts to complete the transaction or agreement would come under the heading, but certainly not amounts that even at the present time cannot be accurately stated and estimated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext:
I have no right to speak again except with the consent of the house, but the position is this: The report by the minister clearly indicated that in some instances the municipalities made estimates of what they would be compelled to pay for direct relief, and appropriations were made by order in council accordingly. Within those appropriations expenditures have been made. There still remains a portion of the aippropri-

Unemployment Relief
ated money that has not been expended. It is to that portion that the Minister of Labour was referring and to nothing else.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can of course bring this matter up on going into supply, 'but am anxious to save the time of the house, so shall just draw my right hon. friend's attention to the fact that what the Minister of Labour now announces is that the government intends to pay, not a third but a half.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext: Within the appropriation.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext: That is something that was not thought of at the time the appropriation to which he now refers was made. I think it is irregular in this way to remove from parliament control over its own expenditures.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext: Since we anticipate going into supply the discussion may be then continued, but I may say, (1) the amount will not be increased; (2) the distribution of the amount is different from that originally contemplated, but as the. expenditures will not foe increased beyond the appropriation and the method of expenditure only is being changed, I cannot quite understand the point made by the right hon. gentleman. The object being one and the same thing, the necessity for making a larger contribution out of the appropriation being brought home to the minister, he agrees that out of the appropriation-which means it will be exhausted more quickly there will be a contribution of one-half instead of one-third for direct relief That is all.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
speechtext: My right hon. friend says he does not understand the point that I have in mind. In a word, it is this. The only opportunity the house has to discuss appropriations and to exercise its control over expenditures is when appropriations are being made. My contention is that if money is needed for expenditure within the present fiscal year, parliament is now sitting, the government should bring down its estimates, and give us an opportunity to discuss the whole question of present and further expenditures on those estimates. I have no desire in what I am now saying to limit the amount of money the government may find it necessary to expend on unemployment relief, but I do submit that we have a right and a duty to control expenditures from year to year according to the well-recognized rules of procedure of parliament.

The ship is not subsidized; it carries
mail and is paid for the service. The position is this:	There is no subsidy being paid to
that steamship for that service but, like any other transportation company, if mails are carried they are being paid for on a poundage basis, the same as freight.

maintopic: EMPRESS OF JAPAN
speechtext: Or by space.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EMPRESS OF JAPAN
speechtext:
Either by poundage or
on a space rate, and sometimes a combination of both, as my hon. friend the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) has said; sometimes it is a purely space basis and sometimes a combination of poundage and space. I think on the steamships it is a space basis, so much per cubic foot or cubic yard.
With respect to the place where repairs may be made by private owners to their ships, I recalled when the hon. member was asking his question making a similar inquiry, not in the House of Commons but privately, and I was given what I at once realized was an excellent answer, namely that the repairs must be made at the point where the schedules of the ships will be least interfered with so that they may be maintained and continued. Whether repairs shall be made on an eastbound or westbound voyage; whether on the outgoing or incoming trip, the place where the repairs are made is determined largely and in fact almost wholly by the schedule factor. For instance, ships are sometimes repaired at Quebec, sometimes at Southampton, depending on the schedules which are usually prepared at the first of the year. If the hon. member will take the trouble to look at any time table of the Canadian Pacific, he will find a schedule which carries forward into 1932. That schedule was prepared early in 1931 or, in some instances, at the end of 1930.
While I have no knowledge of this particular matter, I can only say that this was the explanation given me at that time when a similar circumstance was brought to my attention, and then it appeared to me that the reason given was fairly good. However, I will take an early opportunity to make inquiries, and if the steamship company is disposed to answer-and they are usually very courteous-I will communicate with the hon. member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

speechtext: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: ['I have answered the question, but the hon. member does not like my answer. Mr. Chairman, I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.\nProgress reported.']

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking this opportunity to bring up a matter which would be much better discussed in committee of the whole, where it could be debated and where questions could be asked and answered, 'but I am compelled to do it in this way because of the uncertainty of the interpretation of our rules of late, by reason of which I do not know whether I would be allowed to discuss the matter. There is no item in the estimates referring to this subject which would in the opinion of some, permit me to discuss it in committee, and it is a rather striking commentary upon our rules that while this is not a politically contentious matter, if I want to take more than forty minutes to explain it
Sealing Commission-Mr. Neill

I can only do so by moving a vote of want of confidence in the government, which would invite and indeed compel the government to vote it down. This is a matter in which I want the government to take adtion, but the only way in which I can ask them to do so is by making them vote it down. However, I think by rigid economy of words and possibly of ideas I shall be able to get through in forty minutes.
I wish the government to consider-and to urge upon them-the advisability of appointing a commission to deal with the claims of sealers on the Pacific coast. I use that very broad language because in the past whole classes and categories of these men have been deprived of justice because of a too narrow wording of the situation. I am not asking this house to grant compensation now; that would be ridiculous. It would take me a fortnight to prepare a brief and a day in which to deliver it, and then I would not be any further ahead. I would be only making out what I seek to do now, a prima facie case for investigation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Are these claims antecedent or subsequent to 1891?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Beginning after 1891; I will
explain as I go along. There has been a great deal of misunderstanding in connection with this matter. I will not guarantee my dates or the strict accuracy of my statements, because they are taken from a great mass of involved documents, but the facts are to this effect: In 1886 the government of the United States took it into their heads that the Bering sea was what is legally called a mare clausum, or in other words that it came within their territory and they sought to demonstrate that fact by seizing British or Canadian ships in Bering sea and putting their crews in jail. The sealers, of course, appealed for protection to the British government, and negotiations took place and finally the matter was submitted to what was known as the Paris arbitration tribunal. Before that tribunal the United States government waived their claim of territorial jurisdiction over Bering sea and agreed to give compensation to the owners of the ships which had been seized. This was later done, at a cost of something like half a million dollars. I believe the claims were all dealt with, excepting one small claim in connection with a steamer called the Ethel; with which I will deal presently. However, the main issue was entirely cleaned up at that time, and forms no further part of my presentation.

In the meantime, and while this was going on, the seals were being rapidly depleted by over killing, by Americans and Canadians and latterly by Japanese, who had entered the field. Britain acted for Canada; I want to make that point clear, because it has some bearing upon my argument later on. Then we had not the status of a nation; everything was done through Great Britain, and Great Britain, acting for Canada, incurred certain obligations which we must inherit now at least in some part. In 1891 they agreed with the United States to a modus vivendi, which was that for one year ending in May, 1892, there would be a total cessation of sealing in Bering sea. Great Britain proceeded to carry out her part of that agreement by sending warships into Bering sea and stopping Canadians from sealing. They did not arrest them; they simply turned them out, and of course the sealers made an immediate claim for compensation. It came upon them like a bolt from the blue, and they were subject to heavy losses. It did not seem the financial business of Great Britain at that time, but she put her hand in her pocket and compensated these people. I have not the exact amount under my hand, but it was substantial and, I think, satisfactory.
Then the situation arose which is one of the points I desire to bring to the attention of the government. That modus vivendi was to expire in May, 1892, in the belief that the Paris tribunal award would be made by that time, which would settle the matters in dispute. Along about February of 1892 it was seen that the Paris tribunal would not complete its work in time, and something in the nature of a small convention was agreed upon between the various nations, I suppose principally between Great Britain and the United States. They made some sort of agreement that they would extend the modus vivendi for another year from May of 1S92.
But here is where the mistake was made, in my opinion and in the opinion of people more competent to judge than I am. They did not notify the sealers in time. To make the thing clear, I may explain that the sealing in Bering sea begins in the latter part of June. The sealing schooner that was going out from Victoria did not start in June but in February, because she went down the coast to the Californian and Mexican grounds and followed the herd up north, attacking them all the way up, and finally entering Bering sea. So that the sealers in the month of February had this situation to face. They went out in the full knowledge that the modus vivendi would end in the following May, and therefore they were safe in

Sealing Commission-Mr. Neill
starting out, equipping themselves at much expense to go on their regular trips down south, finally ending in Bering sea, and in all probability not calling at Victoria on the way up. There was of course possibility that the modus vivendi might be extended, but they had no knowledge of this. Now, suppose they had decided, as afterwards some authority suggested they should have done, not to go out until they were certain whether the modus vivendi would be extended or not, in that event it would have been too late for them to set out. And had they not gone out, the answer which any government would have made, had they applied for compensation, would have been, "you should not have remained. The law advised you that the modus vivendi would end in May, and it was your privilege to take advantage of the opportunity which was available." I say, therefore, that they were not notified in time. I do not know whose fault it was, and it matters not. A notice was put up in the customs house at Victoria on March 20, four to six weeks after the schooners had sailed, and then a British boat was sent to Alaska to intercept them and prevent their going in. This was some time about the beginning of June, and then this situation developed. They were again suddenly cut off in the middle of their operations.
Circumstances immediately divided the sealers into four categories. First, there were those who were well equipped, with well-manned vessels of suitable size, and these went to Japan. They ran across the Pacific and sealed there in waters which under the conditions then prevailing were open. They made a good catch and made money. The second group were not so well equipped. They had Indian crews and small boats, and they had neither adequate equipment nor ample food supplies. They were therefore compelled to return to Victoria at an enormous loss. In many cases they entirely forfeited their interest in the ships, the mortgagees and the banks taking them over. In the third category were those who went to Japan and lost money. Whether from a lack of knowledge of the grounds, or for other reasons, they went and lost money. And the fourth category I need not waste time over: it consisted of one steamer. This steamer returned to Victoria, the assumption being that she was not able or was not willing to go to Japan.
There was then an immediate application to Britain for compensation for the losses sustained as in the previous year. Britain took the position that they had received sufficient notice and therefore had no claim. That is a real lawyer's decision. If it had been a case of a mortgage due on a certain date and the date was in June, it was ample time to give them notice on March 29. But under the circumstances, in a matter of this kind, it was not what one would call fair or reasonable notice. Britain is notorious for not being niggardly in dealing with claims of this kind, especially with her subjects, and I do not believe that if the matter had been properly represented to her she would have taken the stand she did. Some fault is due, possibly to some officials in Canada. It was so much easier to write, stating that the matter had been closed, or referring the applicants to this or that letter of such and such a date, instead of pressing forward the matter and submitting to the British government further arguments adduced, indicating the situation as I have outlined it. However, Britain took that attitude. We must remember that Britain was acting for Canada, and for any obligation that she incurred we must be in some part responsible, especially as Canada has since obtained something like a million dollars as a result of the treaty made later. And so far as I know she has not had the grace to repay Britain the money expended in the first instance.
Later on a commissioner, Mr. Justice Audette, took the matter under consideration and refused to hear these cases at all. I do not blame Mr. Justice Audette; his commission was so narrowly drawn in Ottawa as to leave him no alternative. At any rate, he refused to hear these cases, and they have never been given any hearing whatever. But surely every litigant or claimant is entitled to his day in court. These people have never had the ghost of a chance to get their day in court, for the commission never looked into their claims. The commission, as I say, was so restricted that these people received no consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: What year was that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I believe it was some time
about 1914. It was subsequent to the treaty, which was made in 1911. The refusal to hear these claims was based on two reasons: first, it was a British question with which Canada had nothing to do; and in the second place, the scope of the commission was restricted to anything that took place since 1894. And this occurred in 1892.
Now to come back to the relations between Britain and the United States. It was decided by the Paris tribunal, with the consent of the United States, that they had no claim over Bering sea. It comprised extraterritorial

Sealing Commission-Mr. Neill
called this matter to the attention of the government; there was some red tape but in the course of time we got the thing smoothed out, and the Department of Fisheries attempted to stop this practice. The present custom, as we understand it, is that these men are permitted to come into our waters at any time for what is called wood, water, shelter or repairs. The government men were very reasonable and they accepted almost any excuse at first but when it was found that these men were coming in night after night it was felt that something would have to be done. These men were asked, "What did you come in for?" They would reply, "Oh, captain, it is so rough outside." The captain would reply that he had just come in from outside where it was quite smooth. The next excuse was that the engine had broken down, and it is a well known fact that when these men saw the patrol boat coming they would tear their engine apart. The cylinder head would be taken off in order to convey the idea that something had gone wrong. However, the captain of the patrol boat overcame that excuse by putting aboard one of his own men who understood engines, and in ten minutes he would have the engine reassembled and ready to work. That thing went on all the time. Finally patience ceased to be a virtue, and they seized some ships. Four were seized this year. Some were let off on technicalities and others Were taken to the courts, and the lower courts decided against the American boats. The American boats took the case to the Supreme Court of Canada, where the case against them was sustained. It was held at that time that Canadian officials were entirely within their rights in prohibiting the abuse of hospitality by foreign fishing vessels within our waters. Though I had only knowledge of a general nature as to what had occurred in regard to the Sea Belle, I said I was quite sure that none of our Canadian patrol officers would drive these men out to destruction, and I have now absolute corroboration of what did happen to these unfortunate men. Here is a letter that I have received from Vancouver. It is short, and I will read it because it explains the whole thing so clearly.
Referring to an article in the Vancouver Daily Province, in which your name appears.
The article is in regard to a complaint from some Seattle interests about the loss of the fishing boat Sea Belle of Seattle, on Goose island, Queens sound, B.O.-
He means Queen Charlotte sound:
-stating the crew of that boat feared Canadian marine laws, which forced them to take the outside passage on the ocean, causing the loss of the two men's lives and their boat.

I wish to say that during April, I was cruising the coast with the M.S. Forest Queen, on the 8th of April, was anchored close to the dock at Royston

That is near Courtenay:
*-about three p.m., a friend and myself were ashore digging clams. We were also watching a fishing boat cruising Kelp bar, heading for Comox harbour, disregarding all aids to navigation in the form of buoys on the bar. which is well marked. They managed to cross the bar all right, more by good luck than good navigating, and came alongside the Forest Queen for directions up the coast. I was called to the boat by other friends to furnish the information. The boat was the Sea Belle of Seattle with two men and a small dog aboard. They were travelling to Ketchikan, Alaska. They asked for directions through Seymour narrows. On being informed of the course and distance to the narrows, they were quite surprised to find they were twenty-five miles from there. They had mistaken cape Lazo for cape Mudge-
Which I may say was a very big mistake:
-and were going to head up the Courtenay river for the entrance to Seymour narrows. This would show that they were not familiar with British Columbia coastal waters, were lost and admitted it to me.
There is no question that anybody who is going up Courtenay river and thinks he is going up the Seymour narrows is very much lost:
I examined their charts and found them to be United States charts and in good order. The men were sober, and I saw no evidence of liquor on the boat.
They carried two very tall trolling poles, which I advised to be lowered to the deck when they crossed Queen Charlotte sound.
That is north of Vancouver island.
The men informed me they had come through some very rough water on the gulf of Georgia that day and did not think it could be worse crossing the sound (which also goes to show they were not familiar with our coast waters).
It certainly does, because the waters of the gulf of Georgia and the waters of Queen Charlotte sound are very, very different, and if a boat can cross the gulf of Georgia, it by no means follows that she can cross Queen Charlotte sound, which is dreaded even by large steamers. The letter continues:
They asked about the next anchorage where they might stay for the night. I advised Quathiaski cove or Menzies bay. They intended anchoring in Canadian waters for the night, showing they did not fear Canadian marine laws.
As these men had lost their way on the straits of Georgia, it is quite right to assume they had also lost their way on Queen Charlotte sound.
As you are acquainted with the district mentioned in this letter, you will understand I do not intend any disrespect to the two unfortunate men who lost their lives, but like

Sealing Commission-Mr. Bennett
yourself, resent the implication against our Canadian laws. My statements can be vouched for by three other men.
I remain,
Yours truly,
Geo. H. McKinnon.
I may say further, as regards the situation where the boat was found, that if they were really wrecked on Goose island and did not drift there afterwards, they were wildly off their course. Queen Charlotte sound is very turbulent water, and even the biggest boats invariably go u.p the inside passage where it is sheltered. These men did not appear to know that. They .continued up towards the mouth of Hecate strait. There was no reason in the world to go there. A man with a boat as big as the Canadian Pacific liners would not have taken his boat up there. He would have taken the inside channel. That simply shows that these men were entirely ignorant of the local situation.
Canadian and United States fishermen foregather a lot in joint waters, and we do not want even a slur thrown on our Canadian fishermen bhat they were in any way responsible for the loss of these men's lives. This letter from this man, a disinterested party who happened to be there by chance, corroborates the statement that these men, however much we may regret the loss of life, did not come to their deaths by reason of any strict enforcement of our marine laws.

speechtext:
Perhaps, in view of the importance of the matter mentioned in the earlier part of the hon. gentleman's remarks, it would have been bettor had he given the government some notice that he intended to speak on this question this afternoon. The first intimation that I had that he was to speak on the matter was after he opened his address, and I find that no member of the government has been advised. What I am about to say is subject to correction, because I am speaking wholly from memory, but my recollection is that when Alaska was acquired from Russia by the United States, that country, shortly after, claimed that Bering sea was a closed sea. Great Britain took the view that it was not a closed sea, and the dispatch written by Lord Salisbury at that time to Mr. Blaine, in answer to his contention, was I think sufficiently clear to indicate that there was no doubt in international law that it was not a closed sea. However, the claim was persisted in, and finally it was agreed that the whole matter should be settled by arbitration. This dominion retained counsel and presented
its case before the arbitration tribunal which met in Paris, where the British case, if I remember aright, was presented by a great jurist who afterwards became Lord Chief Justice of England. Our case was presented by a very distinguished counsel, and the agent on that occasion, if I recall, was the late Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper. As a result of the arguments that were presented and the evidence adduced by the respective parties, the arbitrators decided that Bering sea was not a closed sea, but that it was an open sea. It then became important to determine what could be done to preserve the seal industry from destruction, and the regulations to which the hon. gentleman has referred were put in force for the purpose. Those regulations contemplated the preservation for all time of the sealing industry, and a division of the annual profits was made by mutual arrangement between the United States, Japan and Canada, and I think Russia, although I am not quite sure about t'he latter. We receive 15 per cent as a recognition of our right to take seals in the open sea and which has been prohibited or interfered with by the regulations.
Mr. NEI'LL: If the right hon. gentleman will pardon me, it was under the treaty, not under the regulations. The treaty came later.

speechtext:
No. The hon. gentleman is talking about another treaty. I am talking about the inception of regulations when the difficulties arose between the late Lord Salisbury and the late Mr. Blaine; but there was another treaty in 1011, to which I shall presently refer. Of course, I am speaking from memory, and the hon. gentleman has his papers in the case, which I have not seen for many yars.
What happened was that we entered into an arrangement with the United States, Japan and Russia by which we were to save, if possible, this sealing industry from destruction. The regulations were agreed to. Undoubtedly they are very drastic indeed. The regulations not only forfeit property, the ships, but impose very severe penalties on ail those who are engaged in capturing seals in the described area. The seals breed on the Pribilof islands, and, as the hon. gentleman has said, the evidence clearly indicates that the seals congregated on those islands are easily killed,

Sealing Commission-Mr. Bennett
and those selected are in the main not valuable for the propagation of seals, and thus the industry is preserved. Speaking subject to correction I would say that in 1911 a further treaty was made. The regulations under the treaty created sanctions which otherwise did not exist and had behind them an international authority. Since that time we have been carrying on under the treaty of 1911. My memory is that the treaty was for twenty years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: It expired some years ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Well, it was for a limited number of years, at any rate. Undoubtedly these regulations worked an apparent hardship at least upon certain Canadians because the effect was to prevent Canadians from killing seals in the open sea to which the jurisdiction of the United States did not extend. It was possible to prevent seals being killed on the Pribilof islands, for they were United States territory, but it was not possible to prevent Canadian boats from killing seals on the open sea beyond the three mile limit, and not upon Pribilof islands.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Except by treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Yes. Therefore this treaty arrangement was made. We undoubtedly sacrificed something. As a country we sacrificed the right to kill seals in the open sea, and as compensation for that we received 15 per cent of the takes, pelts or value of the pelts of the seals killed upon the Pribilof islands. The undertaking was of a mutual nature. The United States was not to kill in the open sea, neither was Japan nor Russia to kill in the open sea, and so by reason of each of the countries sacrificing or giving up the right to kill upon the open sea there was a substitution of the limited right to kill on the Pribilof' islands by the United States only under proper inspection and control, compensating adjustments being made by the payment of moneys to which the hon. gentleman has referred and which moneys have increased as the years have gone by by reason of the herds not diminishing but increasing in numbers and in value.
I recall that during the administration of Sir Robert Borden it was claimed that the regulation had unduly interfered with and prejudiced the interests of Canadian seal fishermen. Mr. Justice Audette of the exchequer court was appointed to make inquiries and to determine to what extent there had been a damnification of the rights of individuals. The inquiry was carried on to find to what extent damages had been suffered by Canadians by reason of the enactment of the regulations in question.

I would again ask my hon. friend to remember that I speak from memory. The date however fixed for the beginning of the accounting or for the determination of the beginning of the damages was the year 1894. I believe the year 1894 was chosen because it was the year subsequent to the determination that the Bering sea was an open and not a closed sea. The very contentions now made by the hon. member to the effect that we should go back to a date antecedent to 1894 weore made at that time. In view however of the fact that the contention of the United States had been negatived by the arbitration tribunal it was felt-and I am bound to say, to my mind with much reason-that the point of beginning was the year that marked the recognition of the fact that the claim of the United States had no foundation in international 'law. After the report of Mr. Justice Audette the matter ended. My memory is that he awarded substantial sums to quite a number of claimants. Of course however there were those who had been engaged in the industry if I might use that word antecedent to 1894. And as the inquiry which he conducted was limited to that date it followed that those cases which were antecedent were not dealt with. The position had been taken by successive administrations that it was not sound either nationally or otherwise to deal with the problem on any other than the basis upon which it was dealt with.
At the moment the position is this: There was a claim by the United States that Bering sea was a closed sea and a refusal on the part of Great Britain to recognize that claim. A clear recognition by both countries as well as by Japan and Russia that the seal industry would be entirely destroyed unless some regulating action were taken. An exchange of protocols, the completion of a treaty and an arbitration under a treaty which decided that Bering sea was not a closed sea; thereafter the right arose common to Canadians as well as to others to take seal upon the open sea. The clear recognition that to exercise that right v'ould have meant the extinction of the industry, and therefore regulations. Those regulations provided that the great sealing industry should be preserved by the action of the United States exercising not only police powers but punitive powers with respect to those who killed seals within the area of sea covered by. the treaty. There was a further recognition that Canadians should be protected by reason of these strict regulations and the granting to this country of an interest in the seal catch from year to year represented by 15 per cent. There was a claim put for-

Supply-Defence-Cadets
ward by seamen and others who were the owners of vessels that they had suffered loss and damage under the regulations, taking from them an unquestioned right to take out of the high seas the seal that they might kill. An investigation of that claim by Mr. Justice Audette of the exchequer court and a report under which payments were made aggregating less than $100,000 if my memory serves me correctly. That is the position to-day. The hon. member now asks that we should appoint a commission to inquire into conditions antecedent to 1894. I am bound to say that as at present advised I can see no reason for doing so, nor have I any reason to believe that the attitude taken by successive administrations in dealing with this question is an attitude that can be properly questioned.
However, now that, the opportunity presents itself I shall make inquiry and ascertain from a study of the documents whatever may be necessary to aid my somewhat faulty memory upon some of these points.
I shall now direct iny remarks to the second matter mentioned by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). In that connection I can say only that the Department of External Affairs, so far as I have been aware -and I have kept in close touch-has received no complaints of any kind along the lines suggested by the Seattle newspaper. At times it is not uncommon to read in the public press reflections upon one's own country by others who do not in any sense understand conditions in the neighbouring country. No representations have been received by the Department of External Affairs nor has the matter been the subject of any communication of any kind so far as I am aware. I am certain that those directly concerned-possibly the relatives and near friends of those who lost their lives-will read with, shall I say, some satisfaction at least, that there has been no failure on the part of the friendly country to the north in the discharge of its duties to all people who. for the moment, seek refuge or asylum within our harbours or on our shores.
I do not think I can usefully add anything further to what has been said in the matter.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I was about to congratulate the Minister of National Defence for having reduced this vote by $100,000, but since he states that he did so with great regret and hopes that the reduction will be only for one year, I think I shall save my congratulations for another occasion. I had hoped that Great Britain having set such a very fine example by doing away with military training in schools, this reduction was an indication of a gradual change of heart on the part of the Canadian authorities. Apparently that is not so. The number of cadets in Canada has increased very rapidly since 1914 up to the present time, and to-day we have three times as many as Great Britain, and, relatively to population, sixteeen times as many. We seem to have a sufficient number of cadets at any rate. As I receive a great many requests for Hansard, I think it might be interesting to the house and to the country to know how our cadet force has increased in recent years. Beginning with 1920, the number of cadets in Canada was 74,991. I have not figures for the succeeding years until
1925-	26, when the number was 120,054. In
1926-	27 this had increased to 126,757; in
1927-	28 it was 133,320; in 1928-29 it was 137,514; and for the last year, 1929-30, it was 137,829. So we see that the number of cadets is steadily increasing, and I think we can say also that everything that can be done by the department to increase that number has been done. I think it is well known that the largest item of expenditure in connection with cadets is that which has to do with the
{Mr. Sutherland.]
allowance to instructors, who receive $2 per head up to 50 cadets, and $1 per head over that number. They also get $1 for the upkeep of their uniform and 25 cents for a suitable military head dress.
I should like to point out to the Minister of National Defence-and I do it respectfully, because I think he should make some note of it-that some of the organizations most interested in education have passed resolutions against cadet training in schools. The first one I want to mention is the world educational conference which, at the last meeting, passed a resolution against military training in schools. Last Easter the Ontario Educational Association passed a resolution against cadet training, which is reported in the Toronto Daily Star of Saturday, April 11, 1931, as follows:
The condemnation of cadet training by a meeting of school trustees and ratepayers held in Convocation hall under the auspices of the Ontario Educational Association will occasion surprise in some quarters, not lessened by the fact that the resolutions committee tried to sidetrack the question.	_
Victoria county proposed that the meeting should disapprove of cadet training in the public school and collegiates as savouring of militarism. The resolution committee's suggestion that no action be taken raised a storm of protest which resulted in the adoption of a resolution definitely disapproving of the cadet system .... The delegates felt it would be inconsistent to display in the schools the words of the Kellogg pact by which the nations, including Canada, renounce their right to wage war and at the same time put rifleB into the hands of pupils and teach them the rudiments of military drill.
I am not going into a long discussion on the subject of whether or not cadet training is military training; I think we are now pretty well convinced that it is military training. I would suggest to the Minister of National Defence that if the government want to promote military training in schools 

and I judge they do-and if certain parents want military training for their sons, the cadets be attached to the military units, which would completely free the schools of Canada from military training. Then you would give the people who want military training for boys an opportunity to have it, and you would leave perfectly free the boys in school who do not want it and the parents who do not want their boys to have it. Then we might open the way for some real physical training, which would take into account the fact that there are girls as well as boys in the schools of Canada.
May I put on Hansard the object of training, as given in section 2 of the regulations governing cadet services in Canada:

Supply-Defence-Cadets
The object of training lads is to develop in them principles of patriotism and good citizenship.
The report of the Department of National Defence for the year 1909 goes into it rather in more detail and says:
.... as feeders for the militia-both for officers and other ranks-the cadet corps are of much value, to say nothing of the other material benefits to youth.
The report of 1910 says, with regard to
cadet corps:
The value of such training from the standpoint of national defence cannot fail to be very great, since much of the cost and trouble of instructional work for recruits in the event of mobilization will be obviated.
It is pretty clear that this is military training, and if so I feel the government should put it where it belongs. These corps should be attached to military units and we should no longer try to spread this military spirit through the schools. The exact training itself is not extensive enough to concern anyone very much, bu,t certainly it gives the boys in school a mind set in the direction of war as a method of settling international disputes. I think in Canada we lay ourselves open to be called hypocrites, if, while we are talking about never using war as an instrument of national policy, and while we are looking forward seriously to the coming disarmament conference for a real reduction in armaments over the world, we propagate military ideas through the schools in the way of military training.
I am not going to direct the attention of the minister to any other resolutions along this line, from organizations such as the Canadian Council of Agriculture, the United Farm Women of Alberta, the United Farmers of Ontario and many others, but I do hope the resolutions of the world conference of educationalists and the Ontario Educational Association might have some weight with him.
I have a communication from St. John, New Brunswick, and also a letter from a minister of St. Andrews, New Brunswick, which reveal a very odd circumstance. The district cadet officer in New Brunswick;' Major G. L. P. Grant-Suttie, offered $100 as a scholarship to the student obtaining the highest average marks in the provincial matriculation examinations. However, students contending for the prize were required to be members of an organized cadet corps for the two years next preceding the date of the examination, and had to be certified by the corps instructor to have attended sixty per cent of all the instructional meetings during that period. The information came to me from Rev. W. Ideson, 22110-183
of St. Andrews, New Brunswick, and in a letter which is rather lengthy and which he does not mind my making public if I wish, he tells me that this man with the complicated name came and ratheT threatened him because he had publicly taken a stand against such a prize, saying it was really intended to encourage boys to go into the corps rather than as a scholarship. This gentleman came to the home of this clergyman and said some rather objectionable things, which the minister says he did not mind in the least. The thing he did object to, however, was that in this insidious way military training is being foisted upon the people. They are being cajoled and coaxed and almost threatened into it. Other correspondence under my hand makes quite clear something I have long suspected, that certainly in some schools where military training is being pushed, boys who do not want to take that training are more or less blackballed when it comes to school sports. Thus the whole idea of school sports is killed.
I feel that I cannot let any year go by without protesting against this expenditure. It is not that I think it will have any effect; I have come to the conclusion that it has no effect at all, but for my own peace of mind, I feel I must say something. The thing is simply ridiculous. If we must have military training let us be honest and say it is military training. Let us say we do not believe what we said in connection with the Kellogg pact, that it was all twaddle, that what we are getting ready for is to fight, and that we are so afraid we will not be ready that we are getting the boys in school in training. Apparently that is what is meant by the department. I would be very glad indeed to have the minister say whether this cadet training is military training; I should like to know if he is one of those ministers whom we have had before, who thinks it is physical training rather than military. I should be glad to hear something from the minister in that connection.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I wish to add my word to what has been said by the hon. member for Southeast Grey, but my attitude is rather different from hers. She expects that nothing will be done; I am going to approach the matter in the expectation that something will be done but also with the determination to keep at it until the purpose is accomplished.
I feel sure that as time goes on we shall have the thoughtful people of this dominion behind us, because the people of Canada are coming to realize that the peace and progress of the world will depend not upon the country that has the greatest military prowess. I do

Supply-De je nee-Cadets

not know whether there have been directed to the minister's attention some rather sensational charges that were made by Major W. J. Wilby, former cadet instructor at the Victoria high school. Because of pressure brought to bear upon him in the conduct of cadet training there, he resigned his position. A report of these charges appeared in the Daily Province of Vancouver of August 27, 1980. The minister will know whether the matter has been investigated or not. The views expressed by Major Wilby amplify some of the statements made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey as to pressure brought to bear on school children to enrol in cadet corps. Summarized Major Wilby's charges are:
1.	In many cases boys are informed by the instructor that they are cadets without even seeing the enlistment form and without knowing of the obligation to be taken by a cadet.
2.	That cadets are not being told of the liability of cadet corps to military service.
3.	Cadets are not told that the cadet service is part of the defence force of Canada and corps are under the military authorities.
In other words, that the boys are beiing enrolled under false pretences.
4.	That cadet corps funds are not accounted [DOT]for at annual inspections and in many cases cadets are not informed of the existence of corps funds nor are they shown any statement.
5.	That check is not made at cadet inspections as to whether all boys are cadets or not. In many eases no count is made at cadet inspections.
6.	That the names of boys are written or typed in a form by the cadet instructors though the form demands signatures. These typed lists are accepted by the district cadet officer and made the basis of payment.
In reference to the foregoing, Major Wilby states: "All this means the paying out of large sums of money from the federal treasury unlawfully."
In another part of the letter the major states: "In an effort to have the pressure, to obtain large numbers at the high school, abated, I interviewed the general staff officer of headquarters of military district No. 11, but was told that nothing could be done. The government's policy was to obtain large numbers and I was to fall in line."
Major WTilby further charges he was requested to persuade all the pupils of the high school who were not cadets to "don the blue jersey and march past the general at the annual inspection."
This, I presume, was in order that the full grant might be made. In the various municipalities of British Columbia attempts have been made to discontinue cadet training. In the municipality of Burnaby they have decided, I understand, not to accept the grant for cadet training and in the city of Nanaimo cadet training, if carried out at all, must be done after school hours.

Now, at a time like this, when the government is bending all its energies towards economy, I do not know of any other estimates in which economy might be practised to such useful purpose as in connection with the estimates before us. This money could be devoted to other things that are urgently needed. The moneys voted for cadet purposes are expended for the payment of instructors, and these instructors are in most instances teachers who are receiving fairly reasonable salaries as things are now. So that you are merely adding to the salaries of people who are already getting a fair remuneration. This is one direction in which the money is spent. It is also spent for uniforms, which the pupils, generally speaking, wear only once a year during inspection.
I thank the minister very much for cutting down the amount of this vote by one-fifth, but I submit that this is a favourable time for him to cut out the appropriation altogether. I quite agree with the hon. member for Southeast Grey that pressure is brought to bear on pupils to join cadet corps. Many of the schools are trying to get away from this and to interest the pupils in other things. In one of the largest high schools of the province where cadets had won high honours in rifle competitions, the principal decided that the corps was not in the best interests of the boys, and discontinued it. This principal, with his staff, recently established a model League of Nations Assembly in which over two hundred high school pupils take part. This was highly commended by the press and the public in both Vancouver and Victoria.
The Minister of Justice some time ago, when matters of peace and war were being discussed in this house, made the statement that Canada was among the first of the nations to subscribe to the covenant of the League of Nations, among the first to subscribe to the World Court of International Justice, and among the first to sign the Versailles Peace treaty. Now, having taken a leading part in these great undertakings to promote world peace, we should go one step further %nd be the first nation to discontinue entirely the training of its youth in military matters.

speechtext:
Great Britain has
already done it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Well, we could be among the first. Many thoughtful people in all parts of the dominion are taking this subject into consideration. At a recent convention of the United Church of Canada, a very in-

Supply-Defence-Cadets
2883'
fluential body, a resolution was adopted with regard to ways of promoting world peace. It was at the Alberta conference, I believe. I quote the following:
1.	Earnest thought and prayer upon the subject of wrorld disarmament that the World Disarmament Conference of 1932 may achieve definite results.
2.	An increasing study of the possibilities of the League of Nations as a great medium for international understanding.
3.	A continuance of the agitation against cadet and military training as being out of harmony with the will to peace.
This is important, coming from so influential a body as the United Church of Canada. But not only are institutions of this character taking a definite stand on this question. I have here a resolution which was passed by the Manitoba legislature at the session of 1930. It reads as follows:
Whereas governments and people in all parts of the world are striving to substitute methods of peace and arbitration for those of violence and war in international affairs; and whereas cadet training fosters militarism and the war spirit in the rising generation; therefore be it resolved, that this house is of the opinion that the government should discourage the continuance and future organization of cadet training in the public schools of Manitoba; and be it further resolved that this house petition the dominion government to substitute for the present grant for cadet training, a similar grant for national physical instruction under a department other than the Department of National Defence.
That resolution was passed last year by the Manitoba legislature. The physical side of cadet training has been discounted by those who are best qualified to speak. An educational survey was made in 1924 by the province of British Columbia, this survey being conducted by Doctor G. H. Putnam, who for many years was inspector of schools for Ottawa, and Professor G. M. Weir, of the university of British Columbia. In making their report they say:
We take strong exception to the plan of having any part of this -work (physical training) done by military officers who naturally give it a military bent. The physical education of children is part of their general education and should be given as such.
The statement was made not so long ago in this house that training of this kind was of value because of the discipline imposed. "Imposed" is the correct word, because discipline is imposed upon those who are trained. I think it is beginning to be understood that discipline of that sort is of very little use either to children or to adults. The only discipline that is of any value is that which is self-imposed or imposed for different reasons than those of the military authorities.
I would like the minister to give this matter his very thoughtful consideration, particularly at this time, because, as I said before, the government is in a favourable position to discontinue this vote without any objection being made by the people of this dominion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
had hoped the minister would say something in reply to the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) and my colleague who has just spoken (Mr. Madnnis). It seems most remarkable that a grant of this kind can be continued year after year in spite of the protests made by a large number of our best citizens in various walks of life. As far as we in this corner of the house are concerned we have stood for years against cadet training and during those years we have seen public opinion steadily coming our way. I have very little complaint to make so far as my own province is concerned because the government of that province is definitely committed to the discouragement of cadet training. It has not prohibited cadet training within the province, but it has been urged to do so by a number of bodies, and it is only a question of time when such training will be prohibited in Manitoba. In the meantime it seems to me to be absurd in view of all the talk about provincial rights that we should have constantly to assert ourselves in order to safeguard our boys from becoming militarized.
The situation is not quite so favourable in connection with other provinces. A number of organizations in Ontario have been protesting against military training. A Canadian Press despatch of April 7 reads as follows:
Colonel Wood, principal of North Toronto collegiate, doubted the value of cadet training. "As a commander of a battalion of militia," said Colonel Wood, "I can hardly be accused of treason when I say this, but as a principal of a school I would not mind in the least if the cadet corps were abolished .... We don't need the cadet corps to develop physical training for students."
As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Southeast Grey, that opinion was endorsed by the educational conference held in this province. I have before me an extract from the minutes of the board of education of Toronto, dated March 5, 1931. This extract was forwarded to me by a ratepayer of the city of Toronto, who asks me to find out from the dominion government why the moneys appropriated by the government should be spent in this way. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the views that have been expressed by the different speakers with regard to the cadet movement.
First let me say that the cadet movement is not a military movement, in spite of assertions that are made from time to time to that effect. I base my conclusion on this fact, that whilst there is a certain amount of very elementary drill in the cadet corps, it is the same as is carried on in very elementary military drill, and it is done simply to teach the cadets to move in a body in an orderly way. It has given rise in the minds of some to the belief that military drill persists all through the cadet movement; but that is not so. The cadets do not get any more military drill than is sufficient to teach them to move in a body from place to place in an orderly manner, instead of going in a crowd pell-mell. They are taught how to turn and march in an orderly way, and that is practically all the military drill they get. In the whole cadet movement there is no idea of an enemy, which is the distinguishing feature of military drill. It is true that the cadets are dressed alike for the sake of uniformity, and that they go through a few preliminary movements, which any Sunday school class could be taught with benefit in moving from one room to another. All that the cadets are taught, and this is the reason for the whole movement, is discipline and respect for authority, and there is some patriotism worked in, in connection with it. I fail to see how that could harm a boy in any respect. I think it cannot do him anything but good. It certainly tends to make him a better citizen to go through a certain amount of training of that kind.
There have been a few specific complaints. One hon. member mentioned a minister in New Brunswick having had a cadet officer visit him and behave in rather a belligerent way.

I understand that a scholarship was given for efficiency in passing the matriculation examination. Surely there is no harm in that, and if the scholarship was restricted to members of the cadet corps, that merely shows that the donor was interested in the corps, and wished to make his gift conditional on membership in it. I cannot see any harm in that. We see instances of that kind every year when the examination reports come out.
The hon. member for Vancouver South mentioned the case of Major Wilby having some trouble with a school board in Victoria.
I have looked into that matter. Apparently the major's contention was that some of the funds had been misappropriated and not put to their proper use. We could not conceive that the school board of a city of the prestige of Victoria would maladminster funds put to their credit. We made an investigation and that was the conclusion we came to. The hon. member for Vancouver South said that the United Church of Canada in the province of Alberta had passed a resolution condemning cadet training, but they do not speak for their church as a whole at all. I have the honour to be a member, a very humble member, of the United Church of Canada, and certainly I feel that it is high time that somebody got up and stood up for what the United Church of Canada really stands for. The United Church of Oanada took to itself a name conveying that it was the church of Canada, and certainly it owes something to Canada. It should stand up for the inculcating in the youth of the country a love of country, respect for authority, and discipline. I think that that is only proper for a church that makes the pretension of being the national church of Canada. There are many people who do not go to the conferences of the church at all, and still I hope they are helpful members of the church, whose ideas however are not indicated by such resolutions as are passed from time, to time. In conclusion I want to say that there is not a bit of organization of any kind connected with the Department of National Defence to encourage people to join this movement. It is simply a matter for the parents of the boys. They join or not, just as they feel free to do. That is all I oan say. I do not think the amendment that has been moved should be adopted.

In obedience to the instruction of the general council the commission reports its appreciation of certain distinct features of the cadet program.	r	,

With respect to rifle shooting the report continues:
Rifle shooting at targets awakens very different interests, entirely unrelated to war, and is a form of sport which calls for such self-control as gives it value in the development of character.
I think that is true. A boy who can shoot straight at a target must of necessity benefit by learning to maintain complete self-control. In a word, target practice tends to the cultivation of a steady hand and a cool head which we require all through life. Dealing with signalling the report continues:
Signalling has proved itself a valuable means of promoting concentration of attention, together with rapid and sensitive response to others.
The next subject dealt with is first aid: First aid needs no argument to demonstrate its high educational value both as equipment for service and as promoting a desirable attitude of mind.
On the subject of company or squad drill I find the following:
Company or squad drill is the only feature remaining for consideration. As to the value of this, there is some difference of opinion, but the preponderant view is that as a factor in the total discipline of the school it is a desirable element.

Both in Australia and New Zealand I was particularly struck by the appearance and bearing of the school children, and with the splendid way in which the governments are carrying on their education. I can truly say of their systems that they instil discipline and patriotism into their youth without militarism. The Minister of National Defence in apologizing for cadet training in our schools said that cadets did not aim their rifles at anybody, so it was not military training. If you have rifles and are learning to use them with the idea that some day they will be directed against some other nation, that is military training. We have not our wars so well ar-
ranged that we know ten years in advance whom we are going to try to kill. All we know is that we are getting ready to kill someone; just who it is we do not know. To say that for this reason it should not be called military is quite the most interesting argument I have heard in this house on this subject.

So far as I know the Prince of Wales has no children, and I do not quite see why he should be dragged into this discussion. Further, the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough rather resents my quoting the opinions of some citizens of Toronto. I have heard a good many members of this house quote citizens of Toronto, Vancouver, Winnipeg and other places; I thought we were here to discuss general policies relating to all parts of the country. As a matter of fact I was born in the city of Toronto and my father and mother were born there before me, so I naturally have an interest in my birthplace. The fact that I moved west is no particular reason why I must speak of the city of Toronto with bated breath.
There is just one other consideration. Before proceeding, however, I might say that the attitude of the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough reminds me of the social worker visiting a woman to give her instruction in the care of children. The woman rather indignantly asked why anybody should want to tell her anything about taking care of children, saying, "I have buried nine of them." I do not know what training the hon. member has given his children.
With reference to the statement of the minister, I might quote the following from the report of the Department of National Defence for the year 1909:
As feeders for the militia-both for officers and other ranks-the cadet corps are of much value, to say nothing of other material benefits to youth.
The report for 1910 has this to say with reference to cadet corps:
The value of such training from the standpoint of national defence cannot fail to be very great, since much of the cost and trouble of instructional work for recruits in the event of mobilization will be obviated.
That indicates clearly the position of the department with respect to cadet training. Recently a woman resident in Vancouver, who has a boy training in one of the grade schools there, noticed when he came home one evening that his clothes were all muddy, and she asked him the reason. He said, "In cadet training to-day we had trench warfare and we went over the top and everything." That is the sort of training the children are getting in some of the schools. In other schools the training is not so distinctly military. I am convinced of that from personal knowledge, because I have had personal knowledge of school affairs in Vancouver for some years.
Another illustration of the military significance of the cadet service is the fact that the department does not pay the grant except where the boys wear the uniforms on inspection day. But why the uniform? Why a military uniform? These things will have to be explained before we can accept the minister's statement. You cannot even hide the fact from the boys themselves.
In one school where some of the boys did not wish to join the corps they offered to debate, with members of the cadet corps, the value of cadet training. The two boys who spoke for the cadet side declared that the training did not aim at inculcating a military spirit, and their opponents pertinently asked "why the defence department should pay for it then." If this does not come under the defence department as a part of military

training, why not transfer it to some other department?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

I wish to support those
in this corner who have spoken against this vote. The difference of opinion seems to be whether this vote is in support of military training or in support of physical training. maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

I had better put it this

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: He thinks it is a vote to provide suitable training for the purpose of inculcating" discipline, patriotism, and so on and so forth. Does he think for a moment that boys cannot be made into the best citizens if they do not put on a military uniform? I strongly oppose such a theory. The hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough rather got away from the subject. In my opinion he did not show any appreciation of it when he suggested that, first, those who criticize this resolution do not know what they are talking about; that, in the second place, they are not family people; and, thirdly, that they do not know anything about bringing up families.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I said that the majority
were not, and I stand by it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
The hon. member may
stand by it, but he is entirely wrong. Take resolutions passed by such very well known organizations as the United Church of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Again I rise to a point of
order. I never mentioned the United Church of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I did not say the hon.
member mentioned the United Church; he was mentioning personalities most of the time. But highly important organizations, including the United Farmers of Alberta, have passed resolutions criticizing this vote. Not that they do not want physical training, but they are opposed to the military aspect of the matter. They are willing to have the money spent in furtherance of physical training in the schools, to make boys and girls physically

I should like the minister to give us the figures in regard to the number of cadets in the different provinces in the last two or three years, to show whether the number is increasing or decreasing.

speechtext:
No one in this house
need apologize for supporting this vote for training. No one need be ashamed to say he supports it, because as far as I know the people of Canada are behind it. There is no doubt that physical training and cadet training go together. It develops the boy's intellect, develops a good physique, teaches him good manners, and disciplines him in a way he cannot otherwise be instructed. maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I would ask the minister to explain just what is meant by non-permanent active militia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: We have in Canada two kinds of militia, the permanent militia, professional soldiers on duty all the time, such as the Royal Canadian Dragoons, the Royal Canadian Regiment, and so forth, and the non-permanent active militia, what is generally known throughout the country as the volunteers. They train for eight or nine or ten days every year, and then go back into civil life.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: How does the minister propose to effect the reduction this year? By training less men?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
The vote is cut
down very largely by doing away with the camps which have been held annually for many years at various places; for instance, in our part of the country, in London. That camp will not be held this year. There will be no non-permanent militia camps held during the year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Then how does the
minister propose to spend this $1,606,000?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The city corps will be given four or five days' training at their own headquarters. There is, in addition, training in connection with various schools of instruction which are held all the time. They will go on as before.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
The minister says that the
city corps will have four or five days' training at their own headquarters. As I understand it, it is not the intention of the minister to reduce the number of men who will train at these city camps. The full complement will be trained for four or five days. That is a reduction in the usual number of days' training of about six to eight, because they used to train from ten to twelve days each year. I would suggest to the minister that four days' training, even though it be in the local unit establishment, is just about useless and practically a waste of public money.

Instead of having the full complement trained four or five or six days, I suggest that the complement be cut in two and that half the complement be given the full number of days' training as in past years. In this way you would build up an efficient nucleus of trained non-commissioned officers, which is the backbone of any militia unit that may be gathered together. I think the minister will agree with me in that. It does seem a great pity that these militia units, which have been built up over a long period of years, and at a tremendous sacrifice to the men who have taken an interest in them-I am sure that the minister himself is one of those who in past days before the great war were interested in these local militia units-should now be practically forced into the position where they will have to disband unless some public-spirited men together with the officers, which will happen in some localities, see to it that the local training camps are kept up and the men receive the usual number of days' training. I do not think that it should be left that way. I do not suppose that many men have gone into training as yet, and so I again suggest that instead of attempting to train-because it can only be an attempt at training in so short a time-the full complement, the complement be cut in half, and half the men foe given the full period of training as in past years. I hope the minister will seriously consider that suggestion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I would ask what the
men in the non-permanent active militia are paid for their four days' training. What do the men get out of it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: It is customary in all city corps, practically without exception, for the pay to be what is called pooled. While the men sign for their pay, the men's pay and the officers' pay all goes into one pool. They do not actually draw it in most cases. By unanimous consent that plan has gradually developed and is now the general procedure. When men go to camp with the rural corps it is the custom that they draw their pay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
If the men in the nonpermanent active militia do not get anything out of it, I do not think any hon. member could stretch his imagination so far as to suggest that four days' training would make any difference in military efficiency one way or another, why spend the money? Would it not be better to keep this money and send a strong delegation, the very best the Conservative party can muster, to the disarmament conference to be held at Geneva, and give what is left to the unemployed? To my
