Supply-Defence-Non-Permanent .
mind it is laughable to give a man. only four days' training. Certainly they would be wonderful men if after such a short training they became efficient soldiers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I am very glad the lady member has added her voice to the many protests I have had with regard to the cutting down of this vote. May I say that she is quite right. That the men have to do such an amount of work and do it for practically nothing is indeed unfortunate. I do not know that I could better use my time for a moment or two than to express my thanks, the thanks of this government and I think of the country as a whole, to the men of the non-permanent active militia who during all these years have kept things going. As the hon. members for Southeast Grey and West Lambton have said, the men in the city corps receive nothing, and in the rural regiments they receive very little. Nothing but a desire to do real public service has kept them active all through the years. The hon. member for West Lambton said that it was hardly worth while to train a man for only four days, and may I state that I agree entirely with his statement. I am sure however that what has happened in the past will repeat itself in the future, namely, that these men in the non-permanent force will give a great deal more than they receive. For years the non-permanent active militia have been doing a work and giving of their very best. A certain amount of that work will be done this year. I should not like to see those regiments, especially some of the city regiments, neglected. While between drill seasons they are not actually drilling, still they keep alive the regimental spirit. I am convinced that that spirit will be kept alive in full force because very strong representations have been made about the vote now before the committee, to the effect that it should not be cut down. We are realizing more and more that the city battalions particularly have not been able to get along on what they are receiving from the government. In many cases good friends have donated large amounts of money. In hard times however that money is not forthcoming, and the regiments find themselves in a very difficult position. Personally I should like to see an addition to the vote, because, as the hon. member for Southeast Grey has said, it is not fair to ask the men to do their work for so very little pay, and I hope that something may be done for them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I can see only one use for a non-permanent militia, namely that if men were paid for a sufficient number of days they would be sure of something and
in that way some of the unemployed would receive a certain amount of relief. Other than that however I can see no use at all in having the non-permanent militia.
I do not wish the minister to get away from the point by saying that I was very sorry to see the vote cut down; on the contrary I am Very sorry not to see the vote cut down still further. To my mind this vote will not be pleasing to those who believe in the necessity for a non-permanent force, and it certainly does not please people like myself who do not believe in the necessity for a nonpermanent militia. The result is that the _ vote now before the committee does not please anybody, and in displeasing everybody we are spending SI ,606,000. To my mind we would be well advised to lay this money aside for the relief of unemployment in the coming winter or for use in the furtherance of other projects for which we require money.
I protest against the spending of such a large sum of money in what really seems to be a ridiculous manner. The minister has referred to "these splendid men." I know they are splendid men. He referred to the fact that they "kept things going." What things did they keep going?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The fact is that the honest, true militia man is one of the best citizens we have.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Oh, quite.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Eveiyone will agree to that. He gives of his spare time and of his money, and the fact is that the Department of National Defence receives more for nothing than all the other departments of the government combined. To my mind the non-permanent active militia should sometimes receive a word of praise from the prominent people throughout the country and from members of this parliament in token of appreciation of the work they are doing.
I am for the non-permanent active militia.

speechtext:
I should like to
make some inquiries concerning a type of activity that has been going on during the last year. A few weeks ago in one of the labour papers in the city of Winnipeg the following appeared:
Under the guise of an athletic club Major Banks, with the assistance of the manager of the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Telegraphs at Winnipeg, has circularized the employees of the two above-mentioned companies in order to have them join the Winnipeg Light Infantry.
I shall now read the circular which was sent out:

Supply-Defence-Non-Permanent
Would you like to join a young man's athletic club? No membership fee. A club with plenty of floor space for gymnastics, indoor ball, volley ball, basketball, physical training classes, track work, boxing, wrestling. Private room for chess, checkers, or cards. Indoor range for rifle and revolver practice. Shower baths, etc. Snowshoe tramps during the winter. Football and track events in summer.
Instructors to teach you radio engineering, telegraphy or signalling with heliograph, semaphore and flags every Thursday evening each week. Open from 7 p.m. to 11 p.m. Also open every Tuesday evening from 8 to 11 p.m. for athletics and games.
The management of Canadian Pacific Railway and Canadian National Railways Telegraphs favour the suggestion that you should join. Members enrolled from the respective companies will be trained in two classes and regular competitions will be arranged if a sufficient number enroll. Plenty of healthful exercise, recreation and valuable instruction of subjects you wish to learn. No expense to you.
These privileges are extended to all members of the Winnipeg Light Infantry Athletic Club. Only one hour per week for military training such as drill, rifle exercise, bayonet fighting, fencing, etc. It is of course understood that every member must take his part in military drill classes when present.
Only boys of good character and medically fit accepted. If you join, you can also quit any time you wish without obligations. Special concert with free refreshments on Saturday, November 29, for members only.
Be at McGregor St. Armoury, corner Machray and McGregor, Thursday, November 20, at 8 p.m. Report to Major E. C. Banks who will take your application. Canadian Pacific Railway versus Canadian National Railways. Enroll now and competitions can be arranged at once.
As this labour paper points out, in the first place it is a very serious matter when such a movement as the one I have described is founded in close connection with an industrial organization. The management is favourable to it, and for any man who will not enlist there is a note of intimidation. As everyone knows perfectly well, for the management to urge that the men should join is tantamount to an order that they must join.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Well, I respectfully suggest that some of the hon. members in this house do not quite understand how intimidation operates; they do not know that if men refuse they find themselves discriminated against.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: It is rather a serious thing when this action is taken. There are also free refreshments and so on. I should like to ask who is paying for all this? Is it the officers?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Is it the government?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I should like to
know who is paying for entertainment of this kind. Apparently this kind of activity is not confined to the city of Winnipeg, for I have had sent to me by the International Association . of Machinists, Montreal, the following resolution:	[DOT]
Montreal, November 11, 1930.
Whereas, the civilized nations of the world have declared their aims to be peace, the reduction of military armaments, the abolition of war and the settlement of all international disputes by conference and arbitration, and
Whereas, the League of Nations, of which Canada is a member, was organized for the purpose of bringing about the above objects, and Canada, in the person of her ministers and representatives has repeatedly avowed her desire to advance the cause of international peace and the progressive disarmament of the civilized world, and
Whereas, the entire experience of mankind has shown that it is impossible to ensure peace by preparing for war, but that, on the contrary, the organization of military force inevitably leads to its use for objects that have no relation to the advancement of the fundamental interests of mankind, and
Whereas, the last great war which devastated the world and brought civilization near to complete ruin was proclaimed to be a war to end war and to remove the threats of militarism from the earth, and
Whereas, it has come to our knowledge that the Canadian National Recreation Association has obtained authority from the military department of the Dominion of Canada to form a battery of field artillery, and is soliciting its members to join the said military organization, therefore be it

I read that resolution because I think it is sensible. It is not put forward by a lot of men who know nothing about war-a very considerable number of the members of this organization were at the front; it is not put forward by a group of sentimentalists; it is not put forward by men who have no children of their own. It seeims to me that it is a reasonable position. I would ask the minister, what- are the regulations with regard to matters of this kind, and where do the funds come from to subsidize recreational and athletic organizations of this character.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I should think the man in Winnipeg who wrote the first letter is a splendid citizen of Canada. He is evidently connected with some signal corps and is trying to get young men interested in his company. As he says, they are only at actual military drill for an hour or so each week, and devote the major part of the time to technical work in telegraphy, telephony, and wireless communication, which is the principal part of their training. As to the source of their funds, as I said, the officers and men contribute their ordinary military pay and this fund is supplemented by contributions from private sources. No government funds are available. All the government does is to supply the military quarters and provide the ordinary flat rate of pay. As to the Montreal battery, it is formed under exactly the same circumstances. Probably some of the senior officers have thought they could do something for Canada by encouraging the men to become interested in this work. In my opinion they are to be heartily commended for the stand they are taking.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
With regard to this particular vote, I join the minister in appreciation of the excellent work that has been done by the officers and men of the non-permanent active militia throughout Canada. For the last three or four years I had the privilege of encouraging them in their activities. Nobody can overestimate the loyal work they have done, and the time and money they have expended under circumstances that have occasionally been rather discouraging. I do not know any group of men who have performed such a commendable public service more faithfully than the officers and the rank and file of the non-permanent active militia. If I may be allowed to speak of the few years during which I had something to do with the administration of the department, I should like to express my considered view that there is no portion of the service of the Department of National Defence which is entitled to greater encouragement than the non-permanent active militia. During the last four or five years the officers of the department, the government and parliament have endeavoured to show their appreciation of that very fine branch of the service.
I want to give the committee some figures with respect to the training camps. These are
round figures, but I think they are accurate. In 1926-27 we trained 27,000 men for nine days, only 7,000 of them in camps; in 1927-28, 33,000 for nine days, of whom 13,000 were eight days in camp; in 1928-29, 30,000 for twelve days, of whom 17,000 received nine days' training in camp; in 1929-30 about the same number as the previous year; in 1930-31 about the same number again, 33,000 of all ranks, received twelve days' training, of which about ten were spent in camp. It was pointed out to me, and I am sure it has also been urged on the minister, that you cannot do very much in the way of training men by giving them only three or four days in camp, and I agree with my friend from West Lambton that the minister would be well advised to reduce the number of men and increase the number of days' training. After all, I submit to the minister that he is endeavouring to spread the training altogether too thin in giving 33,000 men only three or four days in camp; by his method I do not think we are going to get the worth of our money.
I have no doubt that the minister has sought the best advice, but I do not believe it is fair to the service to make it bear one-half of the total reduction in the militia vote this year. Seven hundred thousand dollars is being cut off the non-permanent active militia vote, and the militia vote altogether is being reduced by $1,300,000. So I urge the minister to consider that point of view. A few minutes ago I thought he rather intimated that there might be a possibility of further grants in this respect. He expressed a hope- and generally a minister does not do so without there being something tangible behind his hope-that such would be the case.
I commend to him the work of these officers and men, and for the purpose of encouraging them in what they are doing on behalf of the country I submit they should not be made to bear over 50 per cent of the reduction in this vote. I should like to see it go back to where it was in 1926, $1,660,000. By slow stages it reached $2,324,000 last year. Now, by one cut the vote is brought back to $1,606,000, about $50,000 below what it was in 1926.
I want to say also, in connection with training, that I was advised that it would be good to carry on special schools and if necessary to double the attendance at those schools. I thought it was good business and that was done. I do not ask the minister what is being done this year in that respect, but I believe the success of the non-permanent active militia lies in their having well trained com-

missioned and non-commissioned officers, and I hope that will receive his attention in connection with this vote.

speechtext:
I know that to favour a military vote is not at all popular, and that to do so at this particular time is still more unpopular, but I do think there are more dollars spent in this vote without the knowledge of hon. members than in any other vote in the estimates. I appreciate all that has been said in regard to the non-permanent active force, but at the present time there is a feeling throughout that force that things are not just right, that one arm of the service is getting too much attention to the disadvantage of other arms. There is not a very great reduction in this vote from the vote of two or three years ago, so one wonders if perhaps a little more training could not be done. As far as I am concerned-and I think perhaps I have seen as much training as most men in this country-the system we have followed in the past has not brought the results we should have obtained. A little patch of training here; a little patch of training there; a few men out in one unit here and a few in another there, is not getting us anywhere. I do hope that since we have a minister who is determined-and I know he is pretty strong minded -he will adopt some policy in regard to the spending of this money. We are without a policy at the present time. One year we are up; one year down; one year no training; one year a little patch of training. What encouragement is offered to these officers, noncommissioned officers and men of this country who are trying to do their duty in this way? It may not be approved by all, but there should be a policy under which we could work.
If I might just refer to a vote which was passed before six o'clock, why was that vote reduced by $100,000? It was reduced by cutting out what is perhaps the most practical and most necessary part of the whole cadet training, the uniform. I do not look on this as a little bit of display; I think this money should be spent so that all grades of our citizens can participate in it, and when you take away that uniform from the little cadet boys you bar a great many of the poor boys of Canada from taking part in the training. If you have followed it as I have followed it, you must know that the uniform is the thing that gives equality. The poor boy will not turn out to parade or drill perhaps without shoes or stockings; it was the little $1.25 uniform which made all the boys equal. That is what we are trying to do in the higher schools to-day; we are trying to cut out the

disadvantage under which the poor child sometimes is placed by making a school uniform, so there will not be such a great display of silk stockings on one side and perhaps none on the other. This little uniform you have cut out is a most important part of the cadet services.
To return to the item under discussion, there is a feeling throughout this country that one arm of the service is getting a little bit more attention than the other arm. I think perhaps the ex-minister, who just sat down, is a little bit responsible for that. Without knowing what was being done, hon. members have put through votes of several hundred thousand dollars for mechanization. Perhaps I should not be the one to criticize that action, because I have received a little threat that if I criticized it something might happen, but I do not care. I realize that one arm of the service is of no use to this country without all arms, and there is a feeling throughout Canada that perhaps the present chief staff officer is just a little strong-willed in regard to the course to be followed. In my city we have one unit which goes to training in automobiles; the other unit can walk. There is also the feeling that you could do away with about forty battalions of infantry, I have been told. There is the feeling that the infantry does not count now, that it must be all artillery. Personally I believe you could do away with a lot of these expenses. Why, any day you can read that gazette and find page after page of equipment for units which are not in existence. Of course, it is only in connection with mobilization, but at the present time if we are to cut down our infantry by forty battalions the country should know it and there should be a policy to be followed. If the day has come when a great part of our infantry is not necessary, that policy should be made known, and the infantry should be cut down. The dress uniforms worn by some units are not even made in Canada; they must be bought in the old country. If this government is 100 per cent Canada first, let us begin and go right through the list, with everything we want made in Canada. Hon. members would be surprised to know what percentage of our dress uniforms cannot be bought here. That should not be necessary, I submit.
I suggest to the minister that his policy should not be hidden; it should not be known only to two or three staff officers at headquarters. I shall have something further to say when we come to the vote for the permanent force, and I shall have a word to say in regard to the policy pursued in connection with the Royal Military College, but at the moment

Supply-Defence-Non-Permanent
I have a suggestion to make in connection with training. If we throw $1,000,000 all over this country it ought to help in some way, but I should like to direct the attention of the minister, and also of the staff, to the possibility of putting on winter training. There are a great many single men throughout this country who will have to be fed during the winter. They are without support, because the municipalities say, "We cannot help you; we must only attend to the married men or those with dependents." These men must be kept by somebody, and I suggest that part of this money be kept for what we call winter training. These men might be fed in that way, and the country would get something in return. It would not be a dole, and the honest man out of work would not be ashamed to take it.
In conclusion I should like to say that of all the service, you cannot possibly do without the non-permanent active militia, and sooner or later the minister must bring down some policy and say what we are going to do. If we are to keep on doing a little bit of training here and a little there, I do not think it will be nearly as effective as if we established one good camp where we might have combined training. It might be held in one province this year and in another province next year, so that we might get some good from the money we spend. At any rate, let us have a policy of some kind with regard to the spending of this money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Very well. Far be it from me to enter into any argument with ladies-they will have the last word. But let me say this-and I think it is a matter for fair discussion. Surely we must decide this question: Shall we have a defence force or shall we. not? If we decide that we shall have one, then let it be adequate as far as possible. I know I hold different views on this question from some members in this house, and I credit them with every sincerity. If the hon. member for Southeast Grey does not 22110-184
believe in a non-permanent force, very well. I would gather that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is also of the same view. If I am wrong, he will no doubt correct me. But whait is the situation? The majority of the people of this country have felt in the past, and I believe they feel now, that we should have a defence force of some sort. Let me illustrate. In civic government we maintain police forces. Is there any hon. member of this house who would say that we should do away with our police forces, which are maintained in the cities for definite purposes? They represent force. And so do the defence forces of the country.
There are in this country certain sects who are conscientiously opposed to force of any sort. For instance, the Mennonites, who are a splendid agricultural people. They were brought to this country as a colony in the west and, if my recollection is right, they came under a distinct agreement that as military service was contrary to their religious beliefs they would not be asked to serve in His Majesty's forces in Canada. That agreement has been respected. There is another sect, the Doukhobors, who I understand are also opposed to military service. But people of that class are not in the majority in this country. That is the point. And when the country as a whole believes in a system of military training for defence purposes, then I submit we should not treat them shabbily and they should be allowed sufficient at least to make some decent sort of progress.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre referred to an article that appeared in a newspaper with regard to some recruiting activities of the Winnipeg Light Infantry. I happen to know something about that unit, having belonged to it some years ago. The question was asked the Minister of National Defence-Where do they get the money to provide these entertainments and refreshments? There was also raised some question regarding the propriety of a member of that unit circularizing industrial concerns-the telegraph or the railway companies were mentioned, I believe-urging their employees to join that unit. Let me say from firsthand knowledge that, in connection with all these entertainments, of whatever sort, not one dollar is asked or received from the government. The refreshments spoken of were not mentioned in detail, but in the city of Winnipeg they go around to different companies, the Crescent Creamery Company, Canada Bread, Purity Ice Cream, or some other concern and say, "This regiment is giving a little affair for the rank and file on such an afternoon or evening; how about helping us out?"

2898	COMMONS

And these concerns do come through and help. They also go to the business men, who will put their hands into their pockets and make contributions. That, together with such funds as the officers and the sergeants' mess may contribute, will provide a small fund out of which the entertainment is given. That is the way it is done, and in no other way.
So far as intimidation is concerned, I can say from my own knowledge that nothing could be further from the facts. Let me explain what is done. In building up a hockey team, in an endeavour to create some esprit de corps, one village establishes a team and a neighbouring village will emulate, building upon the community spirit. And it is much the same in connection with the building up of these units. I refer to the Winnipeg unit because I happen to know conditions in my own city. The Winnipeg Light Infantry, in obtaining recruits, will endeavour to concentrate upon certain institutions-it may be the railways or the telegraph companies. A few of the employees of these companies will get into the unit and, becoming interested, they will bring their friends along. It is true that officers do sometimes go to the heads of industrial concerns and have a talk with them. In preparing for the summer camp, the employees having drilled all winter at their own expense and without any remuneration, the officers will interview the heads of industrial concerns and say to them: "You have on your pay roll half a dozen or a dozen men who belong to our unit. Will you cooperate with us to the extent of adjusting these men's holidays when the camp season comes around?" That is all. A man is entitled to say two weeks, and if the camp lasts that length of time arrangement is made with the head of the concern to have the employees take their holidays at that period.
One otiier point. There is a general feeling throughout the regiments of Canada that the estimates have been too greatly cut down. That is natural. But the men are endeavouring as far as possible to meet the situation. They recognize that there is depression and they are reconciled to the reduction of the grant. But regarding the question whether or not the moneys available should be spread out so thinly as to allow only four days' training for a given number of men, or, by taking a smaller number of men, allow for a week or two weeks' training, personally I am in entire accord with the principle of spreading it out. And for this reason. I will grant you that in four days' training-or four and a half, as an hon. member says- not much can be accomplished in the way of what one might call tangible results. But

there is another angle to it, and to get that view you must observe just how a regiment is built up. I am speaking of the non-permanent units. In September or October each non-permanent unit commences winter training. They go to the armouries one or two nights a week, for two hours a night. The officers, the non-commissioned officers and the men attend. These men are paid nothing and expect nothing; they give their time to the militia and to their country. What recompense do they receive? Drilling together and getting to know each other, there is built up a spirit of camaraderie which means something to young people. When summer comes these young men look forward to the opportunity of getting an outing of one or two weeks, and that is a great incentive. The question now arises: shall or shall not we have camps? They are on the qui vive to go, and those who have trained want to go, but if an order comes through that only twenty-five or fifty men are to go from a unit of one hundred and fifty men, it breaks down the morale and spirit of the whole unit.

Speaking first with regard to
the dentists, I think the ex-minister knows from close experience that the old system was not altogether satisfactory. The dentists were employed under the Department of Pensions and National Health, and had this extra work thrown upon them. They were not very anxious for it, and the result was that the permanent force did not get just the service it should have received. I know what my hon. friend the ex-minister is thinking about. He is thinking about a patronage list. I repeat, however, that the service was not satisfactory. There has been a rumour that the turn of the medical corps is coming, that it is now due for extinction, but I have nothing more to say on that.
I do think that the minister and the department should at this time take up one very necessary work of permanent training, and that is the preparation of medical history

Supply-Defence-Permanent
sheets. If some attention had been paid to this matter before the war, this country would have been saved millions of dollars. We are paying very sorely now for what was neglected then. The minister could not do better than see that in some of these schools, which will now be in charge of the permanent force, the preparation of medical history sheets is taken up. Instead of the old system of having a man's attestation in one paper and his medical history sheet in another, the whole thing should be in one paper, because as it is now sometimes we find part of the medical history sheet being lost or part of the other paper being lost, and we are paying millions for our neglect in that respect. I would like to see the minister establish in the schools a special course of instruction in that work and get out a new form of attestation along with the medical examination sheet that would be a little better than we have had in the past.
There is one other thing that I would ask the minister to take up, and that is a revision of the Pension Act so far as it affects the permanent force. The present situation is the most ridiculous in the whole of this country's service. If you are a good man with under ten years' service and you wish to retire for something better, you get out without anything. If you are a man they want to get rid of, you are compulsorily retired and get a pension. Another thing; if a man is a favourite with the service he can get six months' leave when he retires, and if he is not a favourite he may get only one month's leave. That is too much of a haphazard thing. I would like to see the minister take up the Pension Act and make it a real Pension Act applying to all the permanent force. There should be no favouritism. If a man is worth anything, he should get what he is entitled to. If he is not worth anything, under the present system the more favours are thrown to him if he is, as they call it, compulsorily retired. A pension list is made up from time to time to suit just a few. As the ex-minister knows, the act has been amended from time to time always with the intention of helping one person or two persons. An act should be passed to cover them all, and the same privileges should be given to every member when he retires, and no favouritism. I hope that before next year the minister will bring down a revision of the Pension Act so far as it affects the permanent force.

speechtext:
What the hon. member for South Winnipeg said a few minutes ago under the preceding item applies with even greater force to this item. We ought to know what the policy of the government really is.

We are simply carrying on a policy which has been in vogue for a great many years, but which has at least in theory been abandoned. Two years ago, we as a nation signed a peace pact, the so-called Kellogg pact. At that time the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, had this to say; referring to the Kellogg pact:
The very essence of this instrument is that those who sign it ... . begin at once to destroy by peaceful means those instruments by which peace is rendered impossible. . . . We must, therefore, destroy the instruments that make for war, so that when such appeals are made to the emotions there will be no response-no cannon, no navy, no troops. That is the only way by which peace can be made lasting in this world.
That is a clear-cut statement. I do not know whether the then leader of the opposition was carried away by his emotions of the moment. I do not know whether he was making a popular appeal. Personally I would not go so far as he did at that time, because I do not believe that mere disarmament is going to settle our problem. I think there are in the world a great many things which make for war that are more fundamental than armaments. The whole economic situation is much more important than armaments. Then the question of diplomacy and the political relations between nations is of much more importance than armaments. However, the Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, made this unequivocal statement:
We must, therefore, destroy the instruments that make for war, so that when such appeals are made to the emotions there will be no response-no cannon, no navy, no troops.
We in this corner to-night are simply asking that the Prime Minister and the government carry out that proposal. Did he mean it or did he not?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: In what debate was that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
It was in the debate on the Kellogg peace pact. I say that the then leader of the opposition may have been carried away by his emotions, or it may have been a political appeal. I do not know what it was that actuated him, but I think we have a right to ask him, did he really mean what he then said and does he still mean it? Is that what is involved in the Kellogg pact? If so, then it seems to me that we ought to begin even in Canada to reduce the force that we have.
I know perfectly well that it will be said that we have not extensive armaments in Canada. Our navy is more or less of a joke. We have a couple of boats.

Supply-Defence-Permanent
Mr. MERiOIEiR (St. Henri): Good boats.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
They may be patrol boats, but we can hardly talk about them as a great navy. Certainly they would not save this country from invasion. We have aircraft. We have spent a great deal of money on our air force, but I do not think our air force will save us from invasion. On this particular item before us a very considerable amount is to be spent. Now does the Kellogg pact mean what it says? Did we mean what we said when we signed the pact? I have quoted what the then leader of the opposition said. The present leader of the opposition also spoke in that debate. He rather suggested that we need not worry over national defence because there was no one to attack us. He said in that debate on February 19, 1928:
We have no countries to the north of us with which there is possibility of any international difference or conflict. So far as the east and the west are concerned we are Separated by great oceans from any countries that might conceivably come to have differences with us. We have but the one neighbour to the south, and this neighbour one with whom we have lived at peace for over a hundred years, on a policy based on the renunciation of war as an instrument of national policy and which to-day, along with the other nations of the world, gives its solemn pledge that never for all time to come will it resort to war as a means of settling any controversies that may arise.
That seems to be good sense. I believe that was true two years ago and it is equally true to-day. As I have said in previous years, when any estimate is brought before the house most hon. members will ask "What is the reason for the expenditure of this money?" We have still to hear from the minister any good reason why we should continue to spend the money we are asked to spend in this vote. No reason has been advanced, but the vote is placed before us for our approval simply because it has been the practice and we have kept on doing it. Such votes have been made, although at least in theory the policy of the country has absolutely changed. By our very spending however we are showing that we do not altogether trust our neighbour nations. If we were really sincere ourselves and believed that others were sincere when they signed the Kellogg peace pact there would be absolutely no need of armaments and we would settle all our disputes amicably. By voting these sums of money however we implicitly renounce this peaceful means as our national policy. For those reasons I believe that in all fairness we should have from the minister some reason for the continuance of a policy which in view of the pledges we have given and have received would seem to be obsolete.
I suppose the present minister will do as his predecessors have done and fall back on the general idea that some way or another- we do not know exactly how-the militia is an insurance against possible aggression. To my mind that is an absolutely inconsistent position to take, but if the minister views the matter in that way I should like him so so state. One of the hon. members who spoke a little earlier suggested that the great majority of the people of Canada were still in favour of armaments as a means of national defence. Probably that is so, I do not know. I do know however that Canada solemnly signed an obligation to the effect that she had given up that policy. If we do not believe in the peaceful means of settling disputes, we ought to say so, and in so many words. If we are not afraid of aggression from the outside, what is the reason for this standing army?
Under the circumstances I can see only one reason, and that is that it may be used as a sort of police force to keep down the people at home. I do not know why we require a large standing army to watch certain classes of people in our own land. Somebody near me has suggested that we have an unemployed army. I am glad the suggestion was made, as it brings to my mind the fact that a few days ago, according to a press report, troops were sent into the city of Edmonton in order to quell any possible riot in that city. I am not blaming the government for having sent the troops, because I. presume they did it through requisition. I do say however that as long as we have an army ready to crush down any possible uprising of the unemployed we are likely to resort to that army instead of adopting methods which will cure unemployment. We ought frankly to face the fact that we are going to have riots. I said that a while ago, and at present the situation is more serious than ever. I fear that we will have riots next winter unless something radical is done before winter comes. I am not provoking riots-*

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Every time my hon. friend talks he provokes riots.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: In view of possible riots there are two policies before us. One is that we may resort to military force; we may have a sufficiently large force to shoot down those Canadians who are unemployed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I make that statement; we will have to have a military force to shoot down the Canadians who are not employed. That is one policy.
Supply-Defence-Permanent

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
On the other hand we could adopt such methods in this house as would tend to relieve the unemployment situation and prevent riots. I am hoping that the government will adopt the latter policy. For weeks I have been urging that the government adopt a constructive policy, but so far we have had no statement. If the government intend to maintain an army so that it may be prepared for contingencies of that kind, I think the country ought to know it and ought to know it now. If we have to maintain an army for such purposes, we have indeed reached an unfortunate state of affairs. An army is not a police force. I know there are some people who will urge that we need a police force to keep down thugs and outlaws. That may be conceivable, but I submit that an army is not a police force, and in order that we. may be provided protection from thugs, we do not need to spend such sums of money as here proposed.
I wish then to ask the minister if it is his policy and the policy of the government to implement the Kellogg peace pact by making modifications. Are we prepared to decrease our armaments as we expect others to decrease theirs, or on the other hand are we keeping up a big force in order that we may maintain what is generally known as law and order?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: This country has to have a military force, and such will be the case long after my hon. friend and I have gone. Take the League, of Nations itself; if moral and economic pressure are not successful that great body as a last resort has to call upon armed force. My hon. friend said that the Prime Minister spoke about general disarmament. Certainly the Prime Minister made no suggestion that Canada should disarm before every other nation did. When the world is ready to disarm no nation will be more willing to do so than Canada. But it would be the height of folly if this country were to accept the advice given in this committee tonight and toss away our .means of defence when every other nation is showing only very slow signs of doing the same. Canada is not in a position to do that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but I should like to ask how are we going to get this thing going? Who is going to disarm first?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Some country older than Canada should begin the movement. So long as it is necessary for the householder to

turn the lock in his house at night for his own protection, it will be necessary to maintain an armed force in Canada. The minute we reach a state where the people everywhere in Canada can leave their doors open and go to bed knowing that they will not be molested before morning, we shall be in a position to do without armed force. Until then we shall have to have a permanent force, and the one we now have is excellent. The morale and the training of our permanent force is of the best, and as I have often said, a great deal of credit must be given to them for the excellent showing they .made in the last war. Our permanent force was responsible for the training, of the first and second divisions, the back bone of the Canadian army, and to that force should be given the credit. Their vote has not been cut down, because as I say they are. the foundation structure of the Canadian forces. They are responsible for instruction and for that reason we must keep their standard at the very highest mark. As long as I have anything to do with the Department of National Defence they will be kept that way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
The most sensible
suggestion I have heard regarding the vote concerning the non-permanent active militia was one made by the hon. member for Kingston City. If we could gather all the unemployed into an army so that they could be fed and given the opportunity to do the things -the work that needs to be done in Canada, and pay them for it, we might be doing something really sensible. He did not go quite that far, but he very nearly did.
Now we come to the permanent force. I have never criticized this force because of the timidity of my fellow members. I shall be glad to hear the minister tell the committee how many men are now in the permanent force. I am quite sure that if some country suddenly attacked us we would have difficulty in defending ourselves with the number of men that this vote covers. Would the minister kindly state the number of the permanent force?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The force consists of 315 officers and 3,060 men.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I do not think that
such a force could defend this country against aggression. Nor do I take very seriously the statement that the permanent force is maintained to quell riots and other domestic troubles. They may be used for that purpose before very long, but they ought not to be.	'
Surely the government of this country will not let this vote for national defence pass

Supply-Defence-Permanent
without saying something about the approaching disarmament conference and the new attitude the world is adopting towards armament? I deeply regret that actual armaments to-day are greater than they were in 1914, but surely we as members of this house ought at least by word, if we cannot go further, show that we were in earnest when by solemn agreement we said we would disarm. Article S of the covenant of the League of Nations binds us to diasarmament, as does part 5 of the Treaty of Versailles. We have given our solemn pledge that we will do all in our power towards bringing about world disarmament. After a great deal of effort the first world's disarmament conference will be held in February next year. We have the best thinkers in the world on our side. Public men in Great Britain, in Germany, in France, in Canada and in the United States believe, not that armaments will bring about world security, but that disarmament is one effectual way of obtaining security. We have passed from the time when armaments were relied upon to bring security, to the time when we believe we can have greater security without armaments. Should the approaching disarmament conference fail there is no doubt the world will see another race in military preparation, each nation trying to win security in that way, and this inevitably will end in another catastrophe. I cannot reconcile the attitude which first the Liberal and now the Conservative government take with respect to this matter. In some high flown debate the ministers of each government are eloquent in their advocacy of disarmament and measures to bring about world peace, but when an opportunity presents itself to show our sincerity by making a reduction in our expenditure on national defence, nothing is done. The vote for the permanent force is the one I have the least desire to see cut. I would be glad to cut it, but I am not so anxious about it as I am about the preceding vote-the non-permanent force-and the one that follows for the Royal Military College. But I do think it is quite time we said whether these few men are being trained at this great expense of $5,050,000 to defend Canada against some aggressive nation, or whether they are simply intended for a police force. If the latter, the nation can endorse this vote; but if the permanent force is intended to be the nucleus of an army which we intend to organize to fight someone in the future-we do not know whom. at the moment- then it is contrary to the policy of this country declared many times in this house during the last couple of years, that war as an instrument
of national policy is discarded. For the sake of Canada and for the sake of the government itself I would like to have the minister in charge of these estimates make some definite statement. Does he really base the security of Canada upon armaments, as was our policy in the past; or is he willing to support the attitude taken not only by this government but by governments all over the world, that security lies in disarmament?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I want to take a moment or two, Mr. Chairman, to deprecate the statements made by the member for Winnipeg North Centre. This is not the first occasion, even this session, that the hon. member has made speeches along this line, and I submit they can have only one effect, and that, is the very effect that he says he does not want to produce, the effect of inflaming the people to rebellion. It is quite true, sir, and I think it is regretted by everybody in the house and elsewhere, that there is a lot of distress throughout the country at the present time, especially among the labour people. But I submit also that there never was a time when individuals, heads of business firms, heads of corporations and governments were trying to do as much as they are to-day to relieve that distress. I would ask the house this question: What has the member for Winnipeg North Centre ever done in a practical way to facilitate this question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Nothing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Nothing. I have sat in this house many years with the hon. member, and I have heard him make many speeches in times of industrial peace and in times of industrial distress, and they are all flavoured with the one thing-agitation. I do not think, sir, there ever was a man in this house, certainly not in my day, who has done so much to agitate the working classes of this country and has done so little to help them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Ridiculous.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says that is ridiculous?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: No, I say it is ridiculous.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Very well. Then let some of his defenders get up in the house and tell us one practical thing he ever did to make a job for the working men of this country. I have been here a good many years, and I cannot remember a single speech he ever made that would bring to the workingmen of this country even an hour's employment. We hear repeatedly year after year the same speech

Supply-Defence-Permanent
on the same subject that we are discussing to-night. It has become nauseating. One would think at least that he and his friends might clothe the subject in a little different raiment, but we hear the same thing expressed in the same way, only every year it is getting a little more irritating.
Now, sir, have we learned nothing from history, have we learned nothing from the past war, have we learned nothing from the operations of the League of Nations? Why, sir, at the beginning of 1014 what was the condition of the world, what was the military standing of the great powers? Germany could put into the field in 60 days 12,500,000 men fully equipped for war; France could put in the field 7,500,000; Russia 15,000,000 and Great Britain only 6,000,000. Is there a man who knows anything about the history of the war to-day who would not admit that had England been prepared even to a fraction of the extent that the other nations were prepared, war would have been averted? Every man who knows anything about the world war knows that if England had possessed a large standing army at that time and had acted with decision, the great catastrophe likely would have been averted. Are we learning now from the past? What has the League of Nations done? Why, sir, the only article they ever had worth anything had to be withdrawn; I refer to the article which said they could back up their decisions with military force. I ask you, sir: What good is an academic decision in time of war? Is it not a fact that the nation that can talk with power behind it is listened to in the councils of the nations of the world in times of crisis?
I congratulate the Minister of Militia on his courage in standing up in this house and telling the House of Commons and the Canadian people that as far as he is concerned, while he occupies his present office there will be no reduction. In times such as these we must not lose our moorings and our sanity; we must keep our heads, and I say we owe it to this country and to the people of Canada, as well as to that vast army who stepped into the breach in 1914 to save the honour and dignity of this country, to maintain our defence organization. How was this country saved in 1914? It was not saved by speeches such as those made iby the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which agitate this country and set class against class and creed against creed. No, it was done in a practical way; it was done by sacrifice and death. Today the world is paying dearly for that transaction.
I say to you, sir, that this is no place and this is no time for speeches to be made which
[Mr. McGibbon.l
will agitate the people; this is no time for members of this house to be setting class against class. We all regret the unemployment and hardships which exist in Canada today, but I do not think there is an honest patriot who is not trying to do what he or she can to limit that unemployment and lessen the burdens which are being carried. In my opinion it would be much better for hon. members of all parties to sit around a council table and try to do something to solve these problems instead of creating dissension and increasing the hardship and bitterness which is rife in Canada to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
The hon. member who says "carried" is one of the greatest transgressors on the time of this house; he belongs to that class of hon. members whose contributions to the debates are not in proportion to the intelligence they bring to bear on the problems before us.
I simply rise to say that I think at this time party strife should be minimized. There is something for us all to do; we must create harmony in Canada and relieve the terrible burdens which are resting on the backs of the labouring people in different parts of the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
It seems a great pity, Mr. Chairman, that when some hon. members rise to take part in the debates of the house they cannot refrain from personalities. It is all right for the hon. member who has just spoken to discuss the question before the committee, but it ill becomes any hon. member to attack my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre in a personal way. I have never risen in my place in this house to say a word in defence of my colleague; he is quite capable of speaking for himself. On this occasion, however, I feel constrained, as one who has known him perhaps longer than the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, to say a word or two in his defence, because the views he has expressed to-day he has held for a great many years, both before and since coming to this house. 'If there is any private member of the house who holds the esteem of many hundreds of thousands of people throughout Canada, it is my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre. His friends and supporters are to be found not merely in his own constituency but right across the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and I am satisfied that the views he has expressed today on the question of military expenditure are those entertained by a very large number of the Canadian people. And if there is any

Supply-Defence-Military College
place where the views of the people should be expressed it is in this House of Commons; when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre expresses those opinions he is only
exercising the legitimate right of every hon. member to state the views of the people whom he represents. When my hon. friend expressed his opinion with regard to the estimates now before the committee, he was doing just what the hon. member for Muskoka is doing, and it ill becomes anyone to criticize the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre because he dares to express sentiments which, for the time being, are unpopular with the majority of hon. members. What is unpopular to-day may be popular to-morrow; hon. members who to-day are howling for larger military expenditure may in a few years be shouting for disarmament. A few years ago, Mr. Chairman, during my first session in this house, my colleague and myself were likened to Robin Hood because we dared bring up the question of old age pensions. At that time all sorts of epithets were hurled at us because we attempted to do something for the common people. When my hon. friend (Mr. MdGibbon) asks, "When has he done anything for the workers of this country?" I siay I can leave that to the judgment of the workers themselves. I am satisfied that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre 'has expressed the viewpoint of a large section, if not the majority, of the working people of Canada. I would further point out to the hon. member and those who support his views that the present Prime Minister of Great Britain is a gentleman who totally opposed the war between 1914 and 1918, and the viewpoint expressed by the Prime Minister of Great Britain is that of many other people holding responsible positions in other parts of the British Empire.
When it comes to the question of inciting the unemployed of this country against the authorities, I think my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre would be the last person in the world to do anything of the kind. Let me say that the greatest incitement of all was given by those hon. gentlemen opposite who, only a year ago, went up and down the country promising all manner of jobs if only they were returned to power. To-day those jobs are not forthcoming, and the unemployed have a right to feel disappointed and somewhat disillusioned.

Item agreed to.
Royal Military College, $375,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
May I say, Mr. Chairman, that I object as strenuously as possible
to this vote for the Royal Military College. We are back to the same old story; we ought to be looking to new methods for security, but what are we doing? The government of Canada has said officially that we renounce war as an instrument of national policy. 1 want to make that statement as often as possible, in order that we may know that we have solemnly made that assertion. We are members of the League of Nations and I hope we shall be well represented at the disarmament conference next February. We have spent a lot of time talking about new neans of security, and yet we go on doing just the same old things, without giving new methods a chance at all. I have tried repeatedly to have some of the new methods started, so that at least they might run side by side with the old methods. I have tried to have a Department of Peace established but have been told that all departments work for peace. I have tried for two years to have some federal money set aside for scholarships, for students from other countries coming to Canada, and Canadian students going abroad, and possibly to have in one or two universities a chair on international affairs. But in this house I can get support for none of these things.
We were told by the professors who came before the committee on industrial relations last year that we have not in all Canada a library fully equipped for students of international relations. We have not in Canada anything in the nature of a school of international affairs such as you will find in Europe, in the United States and in practically every other country. You cannot induce either wealthy individuals or governments in Canada to back new methods. Yet we go on voting $375,000 to train boys in the Royal Military College. I object to this for many reasons. For one thing, it tends to make boys, if you do not mind my using the term, snobbish. It is a military school, paid for by the people of Canada generally, and most of the young men who go there are the sons of people who could afford to send them to exclusive military colleges if they so desired. And they should be free to send their sons to such colleges if they wish, but not at the people's expense. The people of Canada should not be taxed to keep up an exclusive school for the blue bloods of the dominion. I have absolutely no use for it, and I want it to be known that in my opinion all that money is wasted, and much more than wasted, for we are doing the very thing which we have invariably declared we have ceased to do-prepare for war. 1 have attempted once or twice this year to

Supply-Defence-Military College
obtain pitiful bits of money for worthwhile causes, but have not been able to get a cent. But we' have money to spend as we have been spending it to-night. I know it will be voted, because this is government policy and the government have a majority. But it is absolute nonsense to maintain in Canada a royal military college for the education of boys along military and exclusive lines, while we refrain from doing other things which would tend to promote peace.
It is suggested that we are not going to ensure security except by military means. We do not know. It is like Christianity; if we tried it we might find out. I am not sure that we shall get a report back from the committee on international and industrial affairs this session, but we may be sure that, if we do get a report from them we will win nothing for the house. We shall not be able to convince the house of our position. At any rate, this vote will not go through with my consent. It is a piece of utter nonsense.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Will the minister explain the organization and administration of the college?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The college provides military and scientific training. At the head of it is Brigadier Elkins, who is assisted by two staffs, one military and the other a professorial staff of civilians. Their term is about ten months, the course covering a period of four years. There are approximately two hundred cadets there all the time, thirty or forty graduating annually. The college was established in 1876. I am proud of that college, I may tell the hon. member for Southeast Grey. It is one of the best colleges of its type in the world, and as regards the type of young men there-well, it would do your heart good to see them. If I might do so, I would courteously extend an invitation to the hon. member for Southeast Grey to come with me and see these students. If she would do so, I think that even she would relent. I am afraid they will take it rather unkindly that the hon. member should refer to them as snobs. There is nothing farther from the spirit of these young men or from the college professors either. The students come from ordinaiy Canadian homes and the college is open to anyone. There are no special families who get preferences. It is open to anyone who can meet the physical and educational requirements. There is a large waiting list each year, showing the popularity of the college. Probably 25 per cent of the graduates go into military life, the others entering the professions or business.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Are the military expenses paid by the government?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

It costs the government about seventeen hundred a year.

SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

speechtext: Who compose the advisory board?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I cannot give that information offhand. There is one from each of the provinces, except Ontario and Quebec, from which there are more.

speechtext: Is not that the board of visitors?
