maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
As this institution is almost in my constituency, I am pleased to say that I agree with all that the minister has said. It is one of the most useful institutions in this country. I am sorry that the hon. member for Southeast Grey and others have the idea that it is select. It is not; there is in the college a student whose father was a taxi driver in the city of Kingston, and who had as good an entree into the institution as any other student. All classes are represented among the students. I submit to the minister, however, that the administration is very loose. It is difficult to find out who arranges the curriculum. One criticism which could be made is that this work is done by one man. Who that man is no one knows. If inquiry is made of the officer in charge of education at the college he replies that this man is here at headquarters; if you go to headquarters they tell you it is a man at the college. I believe at the present time they are pursuing the right course, but mistakes were made in the past. The former minister of the department (Mr. Ralston) will remember that in the last year of the course it is possible for some person to change the curriculum. That is a situation which should not be allowed to continue, but I

Supply-Defence-MHilary College
know that my criticism will be laughed at by the people in charge. The matter is important; the government should formulate a policy and not leave it to be run in the haphazard way in which it has been run. I know what I am talking about, and I know that there is not a better institution in the country.
The charge is made that the graduates of this college are snobbish. These boys are taught to go to a certain place, to have an object in view and not to be diverted. They are told that when they are on the street they should go to the comer in order to cross and not to criss-cross, and that discipline affects them all through life. They have received such discipline for four years and you can place one of these boys in any profession, in any industry and he will be pointed out as a graduate of the Royal Military College. These boys are given a preference. Why? On account of the training which they have received. If it is snobbishness to be taught to go straight, to perform one's duty and not be diverted, then I am in favour of snobbishness. To those of us who have watched their training it means the best kind of discipline, and there is no other institution of which I know which gives that direction and impetus to the boy.
The first thing the department should do is to formulate a policy in connection with the commandant. Has the department adopted the policy that the commandant must be a member of the permanent force? I do not object to that, but the time is coming when the permanent force may be unable to provide proper commandants for the college. At times it has worked fairly well, but it has not always been a success. The commandant of that college should be a man who is well disciplined himself, he should not be a man at whom the boys can laugh. I know of more than one at whom the boys have laughed, and the results obtained by the school depend upon the discipline among the boys themselves. There is a very good man at the head of this school now, but who is to be the next? Those who are interested in the school would like to know. Has the department laid down the policy that he must be a member of the permanent force of Canada, or will it be the best man that can be obtained in the British Empire?
The minister has referred to a board, but the only board I know of is a farcical board called the visiting board. If I am wrong the former minister can correct me.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I do correct my hon.
friend; I do not agree with the statement that it is a farcical board.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I have looked over the recommendations made by this board for the past five years and I have not found one practical suggestion. It is impossible simply by viewing a parade of the boys once a year to make a report upon the conduct of the school. There should be a real board, an advisory board. This visiting board is made up of members from the different provinces. Some of those members are my best friends, but they accomplish nothing. A board should visit the oollege every three months instead of once a year. Some of the best men in the country are on this visiting board, but they should be in closer touch with the administration of the college and with the curriculum.
I can only commend this college, but I think the time has now come when it should be linked up closer with the administration. What has succeeded in the past may not succeed in the future, and this visiting board should be replaced by an advisory board, or else have the present board visit the college oftener than once a year and do something more than watch the boys on parade.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
How many
students are there at the Royal Military College?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: There are two hundred students at the beginning of every term [DOT]-the senior class graduates. Some students may fail in the examinations, but the total enrolment is brought up to two hundred at the commencement of every term.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Is the college under the control of the adjutant general or of the chief of general staff?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The chief of general staff for training, and the adjutant general for discipline.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
The contention of
the hon. member for Kingston that the Royal Military College is under the officials of the headquarters staff and that one man arranges the curriculum is not borne out by the fact. They have a board at headquarters to look into the curriculum, and there is also a board of visitors which visits the college once a year.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Mr. Chairman, I have
great admiration for the Royal Military College. I think it is one of the greatest assets to Canada. A splendid type of boy comes out of this college, but I have one criticism to make. This is considered as a federal

Supply-Defence-Military College
college, but the teaching of French is somewhat neglected. I may be wrong, but I understand that the French professors are not paid on an equal scale with the other professors. Despite what has been said by the hon. member for Southeast Grey, I believe military education to be the best possible for any boy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Who is the
representative on the visiting board from the province of Quebec?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I understand it is General Currie. There are two representatives from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and one from each of the other provinces. There is a representative selected by the Royal Military College; the Deputy Minister of National Defence, the chief of the general staff and the chief of the naval staff, all three ex-officio. There is an associate professor of French, Mr. C. A. Chabot, receiving $3,780, which is exactly the same salary the other associate professors receive; also an instructor of French, Mr. J. A. Bleau, receiving $2,940, which is exactly the same as the English instructors receive.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I should like to say just a few words in support of what the Minister of National Defence said a few minutes ago when he referred to the Royal Military College as an educational institution. I have no hesitation in pronouncing it one of the best educational institutions in every way that Canada ever had. It is situated in the beautiful township of Pittsburg, in the county which I have the honour to represent in this house. I have lived within three miles of that military college all my life until I came down here, and I have heard more about war here than I ever heard there in my whole life. The military college is surrounded by a purely agricultural, pastoral, peaceful people. There is nothing warlike about them, and yet they have lived facing that military college every day of their lives. People from all over Canada come there regularly every year on the military college gala days.
The Royal Military College gives the finest education it is possible for any young man to receive, physically, mentally and morally. I have yet to hear of the first clash between the cadets of that college and any portion of the civilian population, a condition that would not exist if the kind of training they receive made them quarrelsome. During their hours off duty these young men come across in their boats in the summer time to the island where I live, and in winter they walk or ride over
[Mr LaVergne.]
on the ice, just for enjoyment. I see a great deal of them and I never observed any bad behaviour amongst them. I have yet to hear of any one of them being charged with an indictable offence. It speaks well for the education they receive.
As to the suggestion that their military training makes them warlike, I say that it is just the opposite, that the man who is trained physically and who can defend himself is never a quarrelsome man. That is my experience, and I have had a great deal to do with the training of boys and young men. Those persons who everlastingly talk of peace, those human partridges of peace or peace doves-where would they be in case of war and our country was attacked? A cowboy mounted on a bronco could not get near enough to one of them to lasso them when they took to the tall timbers. When a man can defend himself he knows it, and is not quarrelsome, but he is ready. That is the way it is with these young men.
It has been suggested that all the students at the college are preparing for war. That is not so. Only a very small percentage of the graduates from the Royal Military College pursue a military career. I did know the percentage at one time, and my recollection is that less than ten per cent follow a military life after they graduate, but they make the best engineers we have in this country. They hold high positions in every part of the empire. No matter where you go throughout the empire you will find graduates of the Royal Military College upholding British traditions. That is quite a different story from what we have heard here and elsewhere about the training these young men get. I tell you when you see them on parade or in doubles or walking singly on the street, the manner in which they do it is an object lesson for the whole world. They are admired by all men and, I might add, loved by all women.
So far as the blue-blooded business goes,
I do not know what that means, but I will tell you what they have, and that is lots of red blood in them. They are not snobs; they are not a bit snobbish. No more gallant young men ever walked the streets of Kingston. I have observed them. I like to see them on parade. I like the strong way in which they walk through the streets. It attracts the attention of everybody. Visitors from all over this country come to that institution, and admire its students in every respect. They are perfect samples of manhood. What is blue blood? I know the

Supply-Defence-Military College
son of a taxi driver who is at the Royal Military College. Would you call him a blue blood? I know the son of a commercial traveller, who is attending the college. Would you call him a blue-blooded man? I know farmers who have sons there, and doctors and lawyers. The students come from the ordinary walks of life. It is wrong to speak of these young men as snobs, and it made me think just how little those who criticized knew what they were talking about. When a man sees these students every day year after year he should know something about them, and I say there is no better behaved class of young men in this country than the students of the Royal Military College at Kingston. I say that without any fear of contradiction, and the records will show it. These young men are brought up right. They get a training that is bound to be good for them all their lives. If I had a dozen sons I would want every one of them to go through that institution for the sake of the training they would get. Not to take up a military career. That is a mistake many people make-thinking that these students are all going to pursue a military career. I tell you that if you want to prevent war you should prepare to meet war if it comes, and the way to destroy peace is everlastingly to talk about peace. Let peace alone and it will come of its own accord. Talking about it will break it up, and will cause war.
I shall not detain the committee any longer. I know that I shall have the indulgence of hon. members for speaking these few minutes, the first time I have spoken. I have sat here long in silence, but I have read every speech that has been made in this house up to the end of last week. I do not mean to say that I have digested them all, because there were many that I could not even swallow. But I have read them, and I could not sit silent when I heard that splendid educational institution in my own riding abused by persons who, I am satisfied, do not know the Royal Military College or what it is doing. To them I say, go and visit it and see for yourselves the work it is doing, and if you fail to admire the young men who are on parade there, then I say you are too hard to satisfy to be in this world.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
From the little I know of the Royal Military College and from the little I have seen of its students, I am in almost full accord with everything that has been said in their favour. It is undoubtedly one of the best educational institutions in
this country. From the little I have seen of its graduates I would say that it turns out not only young men with high scholastic attainments, but young men who walk straight-and by that I mean morally and mentally as well as physically.
There is one thing in connection with which I should like to have some information from the minister. Other than what may be termed a federal university, is this college anything more than an educational institution? If it is merely an educational institution, no matter how splendid it m^y be, we are simply doing what the house has always consistently refused to do, namely, encroaching upon provincial rights in the matter of education. I understand of the two hundred young chaps who attend the school yearly at a cost of between $1,800 and $1,900 each, only a little less than ten per cent eventually find their way into the permanent force. The others find their way into civilian life where their excellent training undoubtedly gives them an advantage. I wish to know whether those graduates form a reserve and are bound to join the colours on certain occasions, or if they are called upon for annual drill. Do they constitute a semi-permanent reserve force of officers, or do they simply become good citizens in the ordinary sense of the term, who may or may not in time of war enlist but who except during the time of their training, are in no way different from the majority of young university students who leave our other colleges? In what way does this college differ from other colleges and universities? How does it differ to such an extent that it becomes a federal institution, and operates contrary to all our constitutional ideas of educational responsibility? I would like to hear from the minister concerning the obligations of graduates in relation to the federal department and I would like to know what part of our defence forces is made up of graduates from the school?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
In the year 1876
the school was founded undoubtedly so as to provide the country with first class military officers. Down through the years a percentage of the men from the school have followed military careers. In the last year 23 per cent of the graduates took permanent commissions, one in the imperial army and eight in the permanent forces of Canada. In previous years different percentages have followed the military life, namely, 12 per cent, 29 per cent, 18 per cent, 29 per cent, or an average of about 25 per cent who take permanent commissions, some in the imperial

Supply-Defence-Military College
army and some in Canada. The ones who do not take in the permanent forces commissions are bound to take them in the nonpermanent active militia. At the time of the war practically 100 per cent of the graduates who had entered civil life but were of military age responded to the colours and went into active service. Those graduates constitute a class who are in reserve as officer material.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Undoubtedly the record of enlistment of graduates is a very fine one, but is that enlistment voluntary or are they under statutory obligation to enlist?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
After graduation if
they do not go into the permanent forces they are obligated to serve in the Canadian militia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: That is their obligation?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Does the educational side of the college come under the control of the Department of Education of the province of Ontario?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: No, not at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Is the minister willing to admit that the federal department does interfere in education and in the affairs of a technical educational institution only ten per cent of which is military?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Undoubtedly the college is a very fine educational institution, and it is conducted by the federal government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Is the other value of the military college a purely decorative one?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Purely what?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Purely decorativecomposed of straight walking and gaily dressed young men. Three speakers have stressed the decorative value, and I will admit that a lack of beauty is sometimes depressing. I am quite willing to pay for some decoration if it is necessary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I am trying to reconcile two statements which have been made but which to my mind are somewhat contradictory. It has been said that the college is not militaristic in spirit; that it is not designed to foster war-like tendencies; that in the true sense of the word it is not a military institution. Yet the college can exist only because of its military nature. The fact that it is a military college offers the only reason-I shall 
not say excuse-the federal government can have for operating a college at all under federal jurisdiction. The federal government must identify itself with the college through military connection. These students being trained in a manner contrary to our whole constitution, in a federal college, the only excuse for which would be its attachment to the military side of. the work of the Department of Defence, I wish to know to what extent the attachment of these graduates to the militia or permanent force is voluntary and to what extent it is statutory.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I shall get that information for my hon. friend, and read it to him. The school now under discussion i3. a military college, and the fact that it is military brings it under the jurisdiction of the domin-. ion. The federal government would have no reason to interfere in the management of Queens university, the university of Toronto or McGill university. The one in question, however, is military in character and for that reason the dominion has control. I shall be pleased to give the information to my hon. friend either in committee or afterwards.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: From the information the minister has given the committee I should judge there is nothing in the British North America Act which prevents the federal government from operating a college or school. In the ordinary case we understand that education is a matter within the jurisdiction of the provinces, but in this particular case we find that a college is controlled by the federal government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: There is nothing to prevent the federal government from operating a military college; we are doing it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: It is being operated as an educational institution, because seventy-five per cent of the pupils graduate into ordinary business life.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I think at this time if the committee will agree we will consider an item of the Department of the Interior.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Should we not rise and report progress?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: No, we may proceed directly from one department to another.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

speechtext:
Scientific institutions - expenses connected with the Dominion observatory at Ottawa, $66,880; expenses connected with the Dominion astrophysical observatory at Victoria, B.C., $25,170.

Supply-Interior

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Would the minister explain the reduction of $4,670 in the appropriation for the observatory at Ottawa?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The reduction covers the four following items: salaries, $57,210 last year as against $52,730 this year; astronomical and geophysical research, last year $7,365 as against $7,400 this year; general scientific maintenance, $4,655 this year as against $4,525 last year; general expenses, $2,095 this year as against $2,450 last year. There is therefore an increase of $165 in two items and a decrease of $4,835 in the two other items, or a net decrease of $4,670.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: There is no decrease in the personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Yes, I think there is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Is the Dominion observatory one of the branches of the Interior department affected by the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces?
iMr. MURPHY: No, the functions of the Dominion observatory are not affected by that transfer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Were any employees
retired from the Dominion observatory?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I will have the information for the hon. member in a moment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I may tell the minister that five permanents were retired. What was the reason of the retirement if that branch was not affected by the transfer of the natural resources?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Under the process of reorganization a few adjustments were made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: So that would be one branch of the Department of the Interior where retirements were made not because of the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The work of the department was not affected by the transfer of the resources, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Were any of the five positions abolished?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I understand that four permanent employees were retired to make way for returned soldiers in other branches of the service, who were thus put into those positions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I understand that five of these employees were, retired in order to enable four returned soldiers to step into their places. Is that the minister's explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: What was the reason?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: In effecting the general retirement of those in the department we laid down certain definite rules, and we endeavoured to take care of returned soldiers, especially those who had dependents.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I am trying to get at the reason why these five permanent employees were retired, when it cannot properly be ascribed to the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces. Why should four returned soldiers be put into these vacancies; was it because of age, or of inefficiency? There must have been some reason.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
The positions affected
clerical positions. The men who were retired not being returned soldiers, and returned soldiers having been given the preference in the government service for a number of years, they were appointed to these clerical positions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I find that five permanent, and four temporary employees were retired from the Dominion observatory. Why were the five permanent employees dismissed or retired?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I have already explained that these men were retired simply in order that returned soldiers might be continued in the service.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: There must be some reason for these retirements. The minister either knows or he does not know. If he knows let him say so; otherwise let him say he does not know. But the fact that there were some returned soldiers outside looking for these positions, does not to my mind constitute an adequate reason why five permanent employees were put out.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Their places were filled by employees who were in the service already in another branch of the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: In the view of the hon. minister that may be an excuse, but it is not a reason. I want to know why these five men were let out. I thought the reason might be the cessation or decrease of work due to the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces, but the minister himself says "No." Is it a matter of economy? This cannot be so because they were replaced. Why were these five men let out?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I do not think I can do better than read to the committee what I
Supply-Interior

placed on Hansard on April 20. At page 718 I stated that the following instructions were given to the various heads of branches:
In the matter of retention on the staff, regard will then be had for preference in the following order, provided always that no employee will be retained unless efficient to perform the service required,-
That is, efficiency is the first test. Then come the qualifications:
1.	Those who enlisted in Canada and saw active service in any theatre of war and who have now domestic responsibilities.
2.	Other employees with domestic responsibilities.
3.	Those who enlisted in Canada and saw active service in any theatre of war and who have no dependents.
i.	Others with no dependents.
Generally speaking it will not be possible to retain any employee who has reached the age of sixty-five years or who has put in the full thirty-five years of service unless such retention is a matter of special necessity to the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
That is no answer at all. I have that statement also; it begins:
The following instructions were given to the various heads of branches of the department when this reorganization was to take place:
Then the minister quotes:
In effecting staff reductions to bring the salary list within the limits of the figure set by treasury board. . . .
That is the answer:
.... to bring the salary list within the limits of the figures set by treasury board, the department will work in cooperation with the Civil Service Commission.
Then the statement proceeds as the minister has already indicated. I want the minister to tell me why these men were let out. 1 understood it was because of the transfer of the natural resources, but now the minister himself says that is not so. The transfer of these resources did not affect this particular branch. Then, in his statement, the minister gives the reason, which was to bring the salary list within the limits of the figure set by the treasury board. I want to protest against that method of procedure. I will make my remarks at greater length on another item, but we were told that these retirements were due to the transfer of the natural resources. There were a large number of retirements made in the civil service which had nothing to do with the transfer of those resources. That was just a deception practised in order to hide something.
Here is the evidence; five men were retired from the Dominion observatory, whioh was not affected at all by the transfer of the natural resources. Out of the minister's own mouth

we have the statement that this was done because the salary list had to be brought within the limits set by the treasury board. I will ask the minister by what means the treasury board arrived at this decision. Did the treasury board investigate; did the treasury board have the benefit of any investigation prior to the date of the discharge of these five employees, by which they might decide to drop them from the salary list? Where did the treasury board get sufficient information to say that five employees should go from the Dominion observatory?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
The transfer of the
natural resources certainly affected the Interior department as a whole; that was bound to happen. Many services formerly carried on by the Department of the Interior now have been discontinued, and in affecting general reductions we adopted the plan of procedure which I read just a moment ago. These five returned men were affected by the transfer of the resources; they would have lost their positions, and in order to retain them in the service they were placed in clerical positions formerly held by others in the Dominion observatory. That was all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Before these returned men were put into the holes created by the retirement of the permanent officials there must have been a reason for taking out the five permanent employees. I suppose I might as well make these general remarks now in order to clear the way for further investigation when we reach the other items. In answer to a question which I put to the minister on Monday, April 20, the minister said:
Because of the transfer of the natural resources to the prairie provinces many people have for the last eight or nine months found themselves to be without a position.
Then a little later on:
Owing to this transfer there is no work for those previously employed in many of the branches of the department.
That is, owing to this transfer of the natural resources. Then at page 717 the minister quotes a letter which he sent to his colleagues. In that letteT I find the following:
The transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces will render surplus to the future retirements of this department a large number of well trained and highly skilled officials of extensive departmental experience.
Up to the moment we are labouring under the impression that these retirements were made because of the transfer of the natural

Supply-Interior
resources. I go back and quote from page 717:
.... no provision to take care of any of these employees was made in the agreements transferring the natural resources to the western provinces ....
The minister was very astute; he endeavoured to lay that other baby on the doorstep of the previous administration. My right hon. leader answered that part of the question at page 719, so I will not traverse that ground again. However, all the time these retirements were said to be due to the transfer of the natural resources. Now let us continue with the minister's statement at plage 718:
I have given to the house the events as they have transpired until the present time. We have now entered a new fiscal year and the estimates of the department show that the appropriations are much less. Accordingly, we have to meet that situation.
Now the cat is coming out of the bag; it is no longer due to the transfer of the natural resources; now it is due to the fact that the estimates of the department show that the appropriations are much less. Then at page 719 the minister proceeded:
In effecting staff reductions to bring the salary list within the limits of the figure set by treasury board ....
There again is another answer from the minister; these retirements are not due at all to the transfer of the natural resources but rather to the fact that the estimates have been cut. That was not quite a straight answer; the facts were not presented as they should have been. But let us proceed and see how far that goes. I hold in my hand a copy of a letter, of which I have the original, retiring a man who had been in the service for forty-eight years, who was seventy years of age at the time and hale and hearty. On April 10 he received this notice:
I regret to advise you that under instructions contained in the memorandum, copy of which is herewith, after to-day ....
There is something ruthless; there is something no one would think would be done in a civilized country to an employee who had been forty-eight years in service, and whose faithfulness had never been challenged. I proceed:
.... after to-day your services will no longer be required.
What reason is given? It is not because of the transfer of the natural resources; it is not because the position has been abolished, because there is no work for him through the transfer of the secources. The memorandum accompanying the letter contains this statement:
Owing to a reduction in appropriation . . . .
That is the reason. Then what further confirmation is there? Take the estimates; when we come to the item we will find that salaries have been cut from $1,500,000 to $850,000. That is why these retirements took place. The minister accepted only $850,000 with which to pay the salaries of his department during the year. He accepted that in lieu of $1,500,000 and then, in order to excuse himself, he comes forward and declares that it is due to the transfer of the natural resources and that, the whole department having been affected, these positions must go.
I was careful in putting the questions to the minister. I quote from page 1300 of Hansard?
Mr. Chevrier:
1.	What are the names or designations of the various branches of the Department of the Interior that were directly affected by the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces?
2.	How many positions in each of said branches were abolished as a result of said transfer ?
3.	How many employees in consequence of the abolition of said positions were retired from the service in Ottawa: (a) on pension or superannuation; (b) without pension or superannuation?
The minister proceeded to give the answer. I have tabulated the figures he has given, and I find this. In the administrative branch there were retired 65 permanent and 9 temporary in Ottawa, 74 altogether. And there was one whose retirement was due to the transfer of the natural resources. In the accountant's branch there were 33 permanent retired and 7 temporaries, and due to the transfer of the natural resources there was one retirement. In other words, there were 40 retirements in this branch, not due to the transfer of the natural resources, while there was only one retirement due to that cause. I will not go right through the various departments, but we find that in Ottawa there were 442 permanent employees retired and 126 temporaries, while there were only 10 positions abolished in Ottawa as a result of the transfer of the natural resources. In other words, there are only 10 persons in Ottawa whose positions have been done away with by reason of the transfer of the natural resources. All the others let out, namely, 558, were let out for any other reason than the transfer o'f the natural resources. And, as I have suggested, the explanation is that the minister accepted the grant of $850,000 blindly and without any investigation. I challenge him to state that there was any investigation into the department to find out how far these various branches would be affected by the reduction of his estimate blindly by one-half. The total

Supply-Interior

number let out in Ottawa is 568; tbe total let out as a result of the transfer of resources is 10: in other words, 2 per cent of the total represents those let out because of the transfer. The total number let out in Canada is 1,295; the total number let out in Canada as a result of the transfer is 461; that is to say, 34 per cent have been let out as a result of the transfer.
Can the minister say that these dismissals have been due to the transfer of the natural resources? Nothing could be further from the truth. The minister can correct me if I am wrong. But I say that these transfers were made ruthlessly and without any investigation by the Civil Service Commission. The minister accepted the $850,000 and was told to cut his coat according to his cloth. To what extent this will impair the service I do not know, but the minister will have to take the responsibility for it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: He does.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I do know, however,
that in no other civilized country has such a thing been done. I believe the minister is quite concerned about public opinion, and perhaps he would like to know what the official organ of his party has to say about it. I quote from the Ottawa Journal of Monday, April 13:
The people who to-day are being dismissed from the service, trained and prepared themselves for it. They thought and they had a right to think, that the words "permanent service" meant something, that, if they performed their work in a satisfactory manner, they were guaranteed security. They now discover that, because of error in the government's administrative methods, the word "permanent" means something else.
This, indeed, the fact that a number of young Canadians who trained for the civil service find themselves suddenly thrown out of work, compelled to start life all over again, is the worst feature of these dismissals. It is a feature which, because of its possible general effect upon the service as a whole, calls for -wonder as to whether it is not possible for other government departments to absorb most of those who are being dismissed.
As to how these dismissals were made, the minister can correct me. I quote frbm the Journal of March 26:
So far as the Journal has been able to ascertain, these instructions are not based upon any inquiries, or upon any conclusions from inquiries, as to how these reductions will affect the efficient functioning of the departments concerned. In other words, the orders have been issued without regard for the problems and demands of administration. There is simply the order to cut. . . .
In any event, reductions of staff, if deemed necessary, and no matter where they are being made, should not be brought about in a haphazard, hit-and-miss way; and certainly they 
should not be made without regard for the human equation and for the effect upon administrative machinery.
There is something more. Mr. Bennett, after all, took office on a platform of providing Canadians with work. That, he said-the provision of work-was the first duty of a government. And since his taking of office parliament has voted $20,000,000 to provide work, and provinces and municipalities have voted millions more. In the light of these things, the seemi-ng policy of dismissing civil servants without much visible discrimination would be an extraordinary apostasy to the doctrines of last summer.
This is from the Journal.
Finally, the saving to be effected by all these dismissals will not be a large one. It cannot amount to as much as one day's revenue. That being so, is it worth while to run the danger of lowering the country's administrative machinery, of lowering the morale of the service, and of visiting hardship upon many old and faithful government employees? The government, after all, should be the model employer; and at a time when it is asking industry and municipalities to spend money to help their workers, the spectacle of it dismissing its own servants almost wholesale is hardly an inspiration.
A better advertisement for Canada, the Journal thinks, would be a declaration from the government, or by the Prime Minister, that this country is not compelled to dismiss its employees, that Canada is not so hard up or so near being bankrupt that its people are unwilling to tax themselves to keep their civil service intact. Such a declaration would be better for the national morale, would be more in keeping with Mr. Bennett's past record, and it is just possible that, in the long run, it would be most profitable for the country. No one wants a top-heavy, over-manned civil service. But neither should any sane person want a skeletonized and demoralized civil service, or a government which, in its dealings with the civil service, acts without regard for human values or for the effect of its actions upon efficiency.
Now we have some of the reasons why these dismissals took place in that way. I will amplify these remarks as we come to the other items.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has stated that he intends to discuss this matter at greater length when another item is under discussion, but I will make a short answer to some of his remarks. The hon. member being a member of the legal profession likes to play upon words, terms and phrases, possibly more than' the ordinary individual. It is true that the appropriations for the Department of the Interior are much less, but every hon. member should know that	the	appropriations	are	less	becausethe services being performed also are less;	the	appropriations	are	less	because
the natural resources have been transferred to the western provinces. Surely it is not necess-

Busitiess of the Home
ary to repeat that in every sentence. The hon. member frequently made use of the word "dismissal," but these employees were not dismissed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I will change that to "retired."

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: In fact they have not been retired, or at least but a very few of them. They have been notified of their retirement, which is yet to take place.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The hon. minister is now playing on words.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: No, the minister is not. They have been notified that they will be retired, but that retirement will not take place until after their retiring leave has expired, and an order in council is passed which is the instrument effecting that retirement. To say that they have been retired before that has been done is to play upon words. In the meantime other departments of the government are endeavouring to place these employees before that retirement is effected. As for any criticism which may have been made by a local paper in Ottawa, the hon. member may be better informed than I am that that paper is an organ of the Conservative party. I have no knowledge of that fact.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Evidently the minister has not been long in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Not as long as my hon. friend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: That is what I pride myself on.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member is proud of his city. That is very laudable; it is a city of which he can very well be proud and of which we all are proud.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
Did I understand the
minister to say that five of these employees were retired in order to make room for returned soldiers?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Five of them, yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I wish the other ministers would adopt the same principle.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The hon. member does not agree with the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier).

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
I did not say that. I was not referring to the hon. member for Ottawa; I was referring to the statement made by the Minister of the Interior. I have knowledge of two cases, one in the Department of Public Works and one in the Post Office department, where returned soldiers, fathers of families- 22110-1851
one of six children and the other of seven- were retired in order to make room for civilians. The principle adopted by the Minister of the Interior is certainly not followed by the other ministers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I cannot answer as to that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
When did this change
take place?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: To which change does the hon. member refer?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: When were these men retired?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: In the observatory?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Yes, on what date?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext:
They were notified of their
retirement some time during the latter part of April.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: How long had these five individuals been in the service, and how long had the returned men who took over the positions been in the service?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: The terms of service varied from five to fifteen years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Does that refer to the returned men as well?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I am speaking of those who were retired. I have not the information before me in connection with those who took their places, but if the hon. member desires it I shall endeavour to secure it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I wish the hon. minister would secure also the ages of the individuals.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: In both cases?

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

maintopic: SUPPLY-SEALING COMMISSION PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS OF SEALERS ON PACIFIC COAST

Why were those five
men retired?
